items.title: xtouch-daemon
items.text: xtouch-daemon turns a Behringer X-Touch Extender into a hardware mixer for PipeWire on Linux. Its motor faders, LED meters and scribble strips control your devices, your applications and the people of your voice chat. A strip can also belong to Home Assistant instead, for lights, speakers in other rooms or scenes. It needs the extender (in MC mode, on USB) and a Linux desktop with PipeWire; there is no Windows or macOS version.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
The device has 8 strips, and the configuration has a slot for each. A slot lists what its strip can show, top first, and states such as "in a call" or "gaming" decide which entry wins now:

[slots]
1 = ["buds if present", "auto"]   # Bluetooth headphones while they are connected, else the next application
2 = ["game if gaming", "auto"]    # the game while you play, else the next application

What a slot names is a channel or a pool. A channel is something you define that takes one strip: an output, an input, a group of applications, a person or Home Assistant. A pool supplies members to every slot that names it: auto and apps the applications that play, people the people of the voice chat, devices outputs without a channel.

So the device follows what you do: the game gets a fader while it runs, the voice chat and the microphone while you are in a call, and the next application that plays takes a free strip. When one strip changes the others stay as they are, and a strip you are touching keeps what it shows until you let go.

Concepts explains each of these words and the ones that look alike.

items.title: What a strip can control
items.text:
• Devices (output, input): an output or input, whichever of several is there, or the default one. With choices, Select switches between devices, e.g. headphones, speakers and Bluetooth buds. See Devices.
  • Applications (apps): every stream of a group of applications at once, e.g. every browser, with presets for browsers, voice chats, games, music and video players. Select can start the application. See Applications.
  • The people of the voice chat: a strip per person in your Mumble channel, with their name, their voice on the meter and their volume on the fader. See People and Mumble.
  • Home Assistant: a strip whose fader, encoder, LCD, LEDs and buttons are entities for your automations, e.g. to dim a light or set the volume of a speaker in another room. See Home Assistant.

Every strip has a motor fader that glides to new values and stays still under your finger, a volume range up to 200 %, an LCD with a label and the volume, an encoder (balance, volume, picking an application, or the media player), LEDs for Mute, Select, Rec and Solo, and a level meter that never wakes a device or switches Bluetooth headphones into headset mode. See Encoders and Buttons and LEDs.

items.title: Tools
items.text:
• A GUI (xtouch-daemon gui): the device as it is right now, every option with its help and errors, suggestions from the sound server, Simulate (what the slots show in another situation), and a preview of the changes, in the window or on the device, before you save. See GUI.
  • No device needed to start: a virtual device stands in for it. See Without a device.
  • Command line: a device test, a check of the configuration with a table of what the slots show when, and why a slot shows what it shows. See Commands.
  • A systemd user service that recovers when the device is unplugged or the sound server restarts, applies a changed configuration without a restart, and leaves the device dark when it stops.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• Linux with PipeWire and pipewire-pulse (or PulseAudio).
  • pw-record (part of PipeWire) for the meters.
  • Python 3.14 (the Arch Linux package brings its own).
  • A Behringer X-Touch Extender in MC mode on USB (see Getting started).
  • For Home Assistant: an MQTT broker that Home Assistant uses (e.g. the Mosquitto add-on).
