items.text: The plugin (integrations/mumble/plugin.c, plugin API 1.0) connects to the socket of the daemon, $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon-voip.sock, and speaks the bridge protocol: the people of the channel on every change and 20 times a second while someone talks (for the levels), and the volume and mute commands back. The plugin's socket thread never calls into Mumble; a second thread makes the calls for the mute, which Mumble runs in its main thread (see the comment at the top of plugin.c). It connects again every 2 seconds while the daemon is not there, so the order in which Mumble and the daemon start does not matter. $XTOUCH_DAEMON_VOIP_SOCKET (in Mumble's environment) points it to another socket.

items.title: Building it
items.text:
cmake -S integrations/mumble -B integrations/mumble/build
cmake --build integrations/mumble/build

makes libxtouch-daemon.so and the bundle xtouch-daemon.mumble_plugin (the library and a manifest.xml, as Mumble installs plugins), the same as xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin --build. The releases have it built in /usr/share/xtouch-daemon/, CI builds it on every push. The plugin header integrations/mumble/include/MumblePlugin.h is Mumble's (from Mumble 1.5.939, BSD-3-Clause, see include/LICENSE.mumble).

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
How the daemon works inside, for developers. To set up the project and run the tests, see Contributing. The other pages of this section: Audio, Live view, GUI, Testing.

graph LR
    Device[X-Touch Extender<br/>/dev/snd/midiC*D0] <-- "raw MIDI (midi.py, protocol.py)" --> Surface
    Surface -- "events: fader, touch, buttons, encoders" --> Desk
    Desk -- "to the controller bound to the strip" --> Mixer[SlotMixer]
    Mixer -- "set_fader, set_text, set_led ..." --> Surface
    Backend[PulseBackend<br/>one pulsectl-asyncio connection] -- "AudioState snapshot after every change" --> Mixer
    Mixer -- "set volume, mute, default" --> Backend
    Engine[SlotEngine<br/>slots/] -- "what each slot shows" --> Mixer
    Backend <--> Sound[pipewire-pulse]
    Desk -- "captures (meter.py), set_meter" --> PwRecord[pw-record, passive]
    Mixer -- "entities of channels, states, slots" --> Bridge[MqttBridge<br/>aiomqtt]
    Bridge <-- "discovery, states, commands, events" --> Broker[MQTT broker / Home Assistant]
    Daemon -- "owns, reloads, stops" --> Surface & Backend & Mixer & Bridge
    Surface -- "what the strips show (live/)" --> Live[LiveServer<br/>$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon.sock]
    Live -- "a JSON line per change" --> GUI[xtouch-daemon gui]
    GUI -- "mode, override, preview, play" --> Live
    Daemon -- "steps (runtime/slots.py)" --> Engine
    Voip[VoipProvider<br/>voip/] -- "participants" --> Engine & Mixer

items.title: Modules
items.text:
The packages of src/xtouch_daemon/, from the device up. Tests mirror them: tests/<package>/test_<module>.py.

Module Role hardware/protocol.py The Mackie Control codec, both directions. Pure functions. hardware/midi.py Finds the device's sound card in /proc/asound/cards; reads and writes its raw MIDI device without blocking. hardware/transport.py How the Surface reaches the device: AlsaPort (the raw MIDI device), SocketPort (the virtual device's socket). hardware/strip.py Strip: what a strip shows, sending only what changed; the motor fader glides to its target and stays still while touched. VirtualStrip: a strip that waits off the device. hardware/surface.py Surface: the connection to the device (again after it was unplugged), its events, touches, the startup and shutdown sequences. Keeps a SimulatedDevice as the mirror of the device, which the live view shows. hardware/selftest.py xtouch-daemon test: lights up the device and echoes what happens on it. audio/ model (AudioState, an immutable snapshot of devices, streams and defaults), backend (AudioBackend, the interface of the strips), pulse (PulseBackend), meter (levels from passive pw-record captures, see Audio), media (MPRIS players, for encoder = "media"). config/ The TOML configuration, validated with pydantic: files, model (Config), sections, slots (the strip of every candidate), the strip types (strip, strips, audio_strips, voip_strips), values, names and presets (Design: presets). strips/ The controllers of a strip: DeviceStrip (ChoiceStrip for choices), AppGroupStrip, AutoStrip, VoipStrip (a person), HomeAssistantStrip, EmptyStrip, on the base VolumeStrip. A controller gets its Identity (entity ids and names) and its Look (label, color, meter, LEDs) from the binder (look_of()). slots/ Channels, states and slots without the device: model, expressions, inputs (presence), timing, states, resolver, simulation, outcomes, why, recording and replay. Pure but for the recorder. runtime/rig.py Rig: the strips of a configuration on one surface (Desk, SlotEngine, SlotMixer), the loop that steps the slots, the requests of modes and overrides and the chord. The Daemon is the rig of the device, a virtual twin (runtime/twin.py) one on a device that is never there. runtime/daemon.py Daemon: the lifecycle (signals, reload, preview, shutdown, systemd notifications) and the requests of the live view. runtime/desk.py Desk: the strips of the device for as long as the daemon runs. Hands each event to the controller (Presenter) bound to its strip and a release to whoever got the press; follows the hands and the chord; runs the meters of what is bound now. A claim ([controls]) takes the controls it names (mask()). runtime/slots.py, runtime/slot_files.py SlotEngine: steps a Simulation (0.1 s after a change, at the deadlines of its delays, every 2 s for the processes), takes the requests (mode, override, pick and pin), keeps overrides, the mode picked (slots.json) and the people (people.json) across restarts, and carries its state over a reload by id. runtime/binder.py SlotMixer: a controller per channel for as long as the configuration, per application of auto and per person without a channel while they are members. After each step it binds only the slots whose result changed. runtime/controls.py Controls: the [controls] of the slots and their entities; the first entry of a slot whose when holds claims its controls on the Desk. runtime/homeassistant.py SlotEntities: the entities of the mode, the states and their overrides, the channels shown and the slots, published after each step when they changed. mqtt.py MqttBridge: announces the entities (haad-mqtt-autodiscovery), restores the retained states, passes commands on, publishes availability. simulator/ The virtual device: device (SimulatedDevice, without IO) and server (on a Unix socket). See Design: a simulated device. system/ processes (from /proc), launch (Design: launching applications), instance (the runtime file and sockets of the running daemon), systemd (notify, journal levels, the unit, the user service). live/ The live view: messages, codec (lines of JSON), server (LiveServer). See Live view. voip/ VoipProvider: the people of a voice chat, with DemoProvider and BridgeProvider (a client plugin on a Unix socket). voip/mumble.py and integrations/mumble/ build and install the Mumble plugin (C). See Design: the voice chat. cli/ The command line: a module per topic, put together by main in cli/__init__.py. gui/domain/ The editor without a toolkit. See GUI. gui/qt/ The widgets (the gui extra): window/, preview/ (the drawing of the device), pages/, fields/, theme/.

items.title: Data flow
items.text:
1. PulseBackend subscribes to the events of the sound server. After a burst of events it takes one snapshot (AudioState) and hands it to the mixer.
  2. The SlotEngine resolves the slots; the SlotMixer binds the slots whose result changed and calls update(state) on every controller, which shows it on its Strip.
  3. The Surface sends only what changed. A fader target starts a glide that moves the motor every 10 ms.
  4. An event from the device goes from the Surface to the Desk, which hands it to the controller bound to its strip. The controller turns it into commands to the backend, run as tasks: nothing blocks the event loop.
  5. The sound server reports the result as a new snapshot: back to step 2.

A homeassistant channel ignores the snapshots. Its entities work as in haad: Home Assistant sends a command, the entity publishes it as its state (retained), and the copy that comes back from the broker changes the entity and the strip. The device's events go the other way: a fader or encoder publishes its number (a fader moved by hand at most every 100 ms), buttons publish events, which are not retained.

items.title: Lifecycle
items.text:
• Start: the daemon starts the surface, the backend and the mixer as tasks and tells systemd READY=1. The device and the sound server need not be there: both are connected when they appear.
  • Reload (SIGHUP, or a change of the file): the file is read again. One with errors is logged and the current configuration stays. _watch_file() polls the file's mtime and size (FILE_CHECK, 1 s) and reloads once a new stamp was seen twice; a stamp that a reload took already (e.g. the GUI's, which reloads after saving) and a file that is gone are no change. Otherwise a new SlotMixer takes over the same surface and backend; the SlotEngine carries its states, picks and people over by id, so slots that show the same keep it. systemd learns of it through RELOADING=1 and READY=1.
  • Preview: a configuration of the GUI takes over like a reload, from memory instead of the file (see Live view).
  • Stop (SIGTERM, SIGINT): STOPPING=1; first everything stops that could show something (the sound server, MQTT, the mixer, the device's events), then the strips go dark and the faders down (waiting at most 2 s), and only then the surface closes. A snapshot arriving during the reset would otherwise paint the strips again. A dark surface shows that nothing drives it.
  • MQTT: the bridge connects (again) by itself. On every connect it publishes the discovery configurations, subscribes, and waits for the retained states with a ping on its own sync topic (the broker sends retained messages before later ones); entities without one get their defaults. A reload removes the entities of removed channels from Home Assistant (a preview doesn't). A changed [mqtt] needs a restart.
  • Status: systemctl --user status xtouch-daemon shows whether the device, the sound server and the broker are connected.

items.title: Decisions
items.text:
• One snapshot for all strips. Every strip sees the same consistent state, and one connection serves eight strips. The strips derive everything from it instead of keeping copies.
  • Coalesced volume commands. A fader sends many positions a second. A strip sets only the latest one when the previous command finished, and shows it at once, so the display does not lag behind the hand.
  • The default device follows by name. A strip without device looks up the default in every snapshot, so it and its meter follow a switch of the default.
  • One owner per strip. A strip belongs to the sound server or to Home Assistant, by its type; two sources would fight over the motor.
  • Availability follows the device. The entities are available while the daemon runs and the device is connected, so Home Assistant greys out controls that would do nothing. A last will covers a crash.
  • haad-mqtt-autodiscovery as a path dependency, as in haad: the same entities, from a checkout next to this one (which also sets Python 3.14).
  • No volume restore. The sound server keeps the volumes. The daemon remembers only the volume of an idle application strip, for its next stream, while it runs.
  • Channels, states and slots (design): the SlotEngine alone decides what shows where (the pick encoder and pins are requests to it), the SlotMixer only shows it. Slots held on the Desk are fixed inputs of the resolver, so nothing changes under a finger. A slot that shows something else flashes its label and why for switching.banner seconds; a new mode shows its banner across the LCDs instead.

items.title: Audio
items.text: How the daemon reads the sound server and measures the meters (audio/).

items.title: The meters
items.text:
• Passive, native captures. The meters use pw-record with node.passive = true: a capture never wakes a device, never lights the microphone indicator, and never switches Bluetooth headphones into headset mode.
  • Native PipeWire streams on purpose. WirePlumber 0.5.18 (PipeWire 1.6.10) restores captures of PulseAudio clients (parec, peak detection streams) at 0 % volume, so those would only get silence.
  • state.restore-props = false keeps WirePlumber from saving the captures at all.
  • node.dont-reconnect = true keeps a capture with its device or stream. WirePlumber makes a stream whose target is the default when it is linked follow the default (like PulseAudio), so without it the meter of the default output would show the next default output after Select.
  • Unbuffered. pw-record runs under stdbuf -o0 (coreutils). Buffered, its output comes in blocks of 4096 bytes (64 ms at 8 kHz), so the meters lagged and two meters of the same audio differed by up to that much. Unbuffered, it writes every cycle of the graph; the daemon takes the peak of every 20 ms.
  • Stall restart. WirePlumber links a passive capture only once and gives up when that fails, e.g. while Bluetooth headphones disappear and streams move. A capture that gets no audio for 3 s while its device or stream plays is started again.

items.title: Meter points from the volume
items.text:
Measured with PipeWire 1.6.10: a tone into a null sink, the volume and Mute of the test stream and sink set with pw-cli set-param.

  • A playback stream and an input apply their volume and Mute in their own node (audioconvert's channel mixer), before their output ports, so every capture of them is after both.
  • audioconvert has monitor ports only on nodes with input ports (outputs, capture streams), not on playback streams or inputs, so there is no tap before the volume. node.passive changes only the scheduling.
  • The monitor of an output is before its volume and Mute (monitorVolumes and monitorMute stay untouched unless monitor.channel-volumes is on).
  • pipewire-pulse turns a PulseAudio volume v into the linear channel volume v³ (50 % is 0.125).

So the meters capture what they can and scale it with the volume the sound server tells (meter.scale_of()):

  • pre-fader divides the audio of a stream or input by v³. The audio of a muted stream or input is gone, and its pre-fader level with it.
  • post-fader multiplies the monitor of an output by v³ (0 while muted).
  • The volume news is ahead of the captured audio, so after a change the division uses the loudest of the volumes of the last 0.3 s (GAIN_SETTLE): a fader pulled down must not light the clip LED.

Reference: spa/plugins/audioconvert/audioconvert.c (monitor ports in reconfigure_mode() only for SPA_DIRECTION_INPUT; the monitor volume in impl_node_process()).

items.title: GUI
items.text: xtouch-daemon gui is an optional editor for the configuration file, in the subpackage gui and the extra of the same name, like the GUI of openhasp-config-manager. The daemon itself does not import it. How to use it: GUI.

items.title: Layers
items.text:
• Toolkit-free domain, thin widgets. gui/domain decides everything, gui/qt only shows it and passes edits back:
  • slots_document: the file as plain values, validated with parse_config() (the messages of check-config), and saved;
  • slot_stacks: the stacks of the slots as rows to edit; simulate and slots.outcomes: what other modes and states would show;
  • looks: how the live view draws each strip; status: whether the device runs the saved file;
  • sources: suggestions from the sound server; problems: which page shows a problem;
  • apply(): reload, restart or "the daemon does not run".
  • One source of truth: the Editor (qt/editor.py) holds the document, its history and its validation. Views read from it and change the document only through it, so nothing keeps a copy that could go stale. Its signal changed(Change) comes once per edit, after the document was validated once.
  • Changes say what changed. A Change (gui/domain/changes.py) has a Scope and, for some scopes, a path. Each page's show_document(change) updates only what that scope touches.
Scope What changed VALUE A value in place; the field that made it shows it already. CHANNELS, STATES A channel or state was added, removed, renamed or duplicated. SLOTS A candidate of a stack was added, removed, moved or changed. SECTION A section was added or removed. ALIASES The list of aliases. DOCUMENT Anything (undo, redo, revert). FILE The file was written, so the document is the same.

items.title: The window
items.text:
• Pages by what they edit. A rail (gui/qt/window/rail.py) has the pages Slots (a card per slot with its stack, an inspector for the candidate picked, why it shows, Simulate), Channels, States and Settings ([device], [behavior], [aliases], [mqtt] as "Home Assistant", [voip]). Slots, Channels and States are two panes with a PaneSplitter (gui/qt/window/splitter.py) that keeps its share in QSettings.
  • The device on every page. The drawing of the device (DeviceView, gui/qt/window/device_view.py) and the pages with their rail are QDockWidgets: one above the other at first, at any side, or windows of their own; QMainWindow.saveState() keeps where they are. The central widget is an empty placeholder, so the docks have all the room. The header and the footer are fixed QToolBars, so they reach across the window. A click on a strip of the drawing picks its slot on the page Slots. The menus hold what is used now and then (the theme, the zoom) and the keys of the window.
  • Previews of the controls. gui/domain/demos.py makes a short scene per part of a strip from the values in the form; PartPreview (gui/qt/preview/part_view.py) shows it in a StripView cut to the part. See Design: previews of the controls.
  • Undo instead of questions. History (gui/domain/history.py) keeps the states of the document before every edit, so removing a channel or reverting the file asks nothing and Ctrl+Z brings it back. Typing into one option is one step. Ctrl+Z undoes in the document also while a text field has the focus (gui/qt/window/input_filter.py, which also keeps the wheel from changing a field under the mouse).

items.title: Forms
items.text:
• From the models. gui/domain/schema.py reads the options of every section and channel type from the pydantic models: the type picks the widget (switch, number, choice, color swatches, list chips, masked secret, file), the attribute docstrings become the help, Field constraints the ranges, Meanings next to a choice (config/values.py) say what each value does, and Presets on a list of names makes it suggest the presets of its kind. A new option or channel type needs no GUI code; a test fails for an option without help or a value without a meaning. gui/domain/docs.py holds the "Learn more" links into this site, and a test checks each against the headings of docs/.
  • In the order of the device. A channel's form lists its options from top to bottom like its strip: what it controls, the encoder and its ring, the LCD, the meter, the buttons, the fader and the range of the volume, the id. This is STRIP_OPTION_ORDER in gui/domain/schema.py, apart from the order of the fields in config/; a test fails for an option without a place in it.
  • The comments stay. Saving writes the changes into the TOML document with tomlkit: unchanged values keep their place, their comments and their form (a stack as a string, a list or tables), and a renamed channel keeps its table. The file is written in place, so a symlinked configuration stays one.

items.title: Drawing and updating
items.text:
• Built once, updated in place. The pages build their widgets once, and showing the document loads the values into them (OptionRow.load()); no page is cleared and built again. A part that comes and goes (an absent section, the form of each channel type) is a page of a Stack sized to its current part, not a widget shown and hidden.
  • No layout for what stays the same. Showing the document again, or a live update with every change of the device, changes no geometry when nothing differs: set_text and the tab texts are set only when they differ, theme.set_role restyles only for another role, and the list chips stay while their values are the same. Icons are kept with their name and color (theme.set_icon), so a new theme draws them again (theme.refresh_icons) without building a page.
  • One visual system. qt/theme/ holds the design tokens: the colors of the dark and the light theme (text at 4.5:1 or more and the outlines of controls at 3:1 or more on every surface, WCAG 2.2 AA, checked by the tests), a 4 px spacing scale, radii, the height of controls, a type scale relative to the desktop font, and the colors of the device for the drawing, the same in both themes. Widgets set style roles (theme.set_role) and take their sizes from the tokens instead of styling themselves. The drawing decides what a strip shows (a StripFace) apart from painting it.

items.title: The daemon
items.text:
• Found, not guessed. xtouch-daemon run writes $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon.json (its process id, its configuration file, whether systemd started it) while it runs (system/instance.py), so the GUI finds it wherever it was started, and a second daemon names the one that has the device.
  • Applying a file. A saved file is reloaded (SIGHUP) only when the daemon reads that file. A changed [mqtt] needs a restart, since a reload doesn't take it (another [device] name or virtual it does: Surface.use). The GUI restarts only the service: systemd.Service (shared with install-service) reads the state of the unit and installs, starts and restarts it.

items.title: PyQt6, QtAwesome and qt-themes
items.text: The same as openhasp-config-manager, so the tools look and work alike. The wheels carry Qt itself, so uv tool install needs no system packages (GTK 4 through PyGObject needs the system libraries and a compiler); Qt paints the drawing of the device with QPainter and does drag and drop; pytest-qt runs the widgets offscreen.

items.title: Live view
items.text: The GUI shows the strips as the device shows them right now, which only the daemon knows. xtouch-daemon run serves that on the Unix socket $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon.sock (mode 0600, next to the runtime file of system/instance.py) for as long as it runs (live/).

items.title: Snapshots
items.text:
• Whole states, one JSON line each. A client gets the whole state when it connects and again whenever something changed. A line is about 2 KB; a state rather than changes means a client that connects late or misses one needs nothing else. version changes when a line means something else; new fields are optional with a default, so they keep it.
  • Pushed, not polled. Nothing runs on a timer: what changes a snapshot calls LiveServer.changed() (the Surface for every message to and from the device and its connection, the sound server, the voice chat, each step of the slots, the MQTT bridge, the requests, a reload and the end of a preview). The snapshot goes out once the event loop is through with what it does at that moment, so what changes together goes out together, as often as things change. One that tells nothing new (see below) is not sent. The views of the twins go out the same way, from their own surfaces and steps; reality reaches a twin when it changes.
  • What moves by itself is told once. A meter is sent with the level it was set to and when (meter_at), a fader that glides with its position, speed and target then (Glide), as time.monotonic(), which is the same clock in the GUI on this machine. The GUI draws the fall and the glide at the rate of the screen (meter_now(), fader_now(), the same steps as the daemon's motor drive, hardware.strip.glide_step()); a snapshot that differs only in where a glide is now (steady()) is not sent. So a moving fader costs a line when it starts and one when it arrives, a meter a line per peak (10 a second while it plays), a dark meter none.
  • What it has:
  • the strips: the LCD lines and backlight, the LEDs, the ring, the fader and whether it is touched, the meter. They are the Surface's mirror of the device (a SimulatedDevice): what reached it, with the motors and meters moving as on the device;
  • whether the device, the sound server and the broker are connected, and whether the device is the virtual one;
  • the fingerprint() of the configuration in use;
  • slots (SlotsState): the mode and the one picked by hand; per slot the candidate, channel, pool, member and why; per state its value, since, source and override; per pool the members that wait;
  • preview, simulated and features (what the daemon takes: mode, override, play, preview, situation, twin).
  • The devices it saw. A line of its own, {"known_devices": [...]} (KnownDevices), when a client connects (if there are any) and whenever they change: every output and input the sound server had, with its card, the profile the card was in and when it was there last (runtime/device_memory.py, kept in devices.json of the state directory, forgotten after 90 days). The GUI suggests them while they are not there; the CLI skips the line.
  • Applied or not. The fingerprint is a hash of the whole configuration (secrets included). The GUI compares it with the one of the saved file, so it can say whether the daemon took the file instead of assuming a reload worked (it keeps the old configuration when the new one has errors or a changed [mqtt]).

items.title: Requests
items.text:
A client may send requests, a line of JSON each. Otherwise the GUI changes the daemon through the file and a reload.

Request What {"request": "mode", "mode": "gaming"} Picks a mode (auto gives it back to the rules, "+1" the next). {"request": "override", "state": "call", "value": "on"} Overrides a state (auto, on, off). {"request": "play", "event": "fader_moved", "strip": 2, "value": 8000} A hand from the GUI: taken by the Surface as if the device sent it (Surface.play()), while a device is connected. Also fader_touched (touched), button_pressed (button, its note, and pressed), encoder_turned (steps), encoder_pressed (pressed). No answer. {"request": "forget_device", "name": "bluez_output.1", "direction": "output"} Forgets a device it saw (Delete in the list of the GUI). The clients get the devices again. No answer. StartPreview, KeepPreview, EndPreview The live preview.
  • Of the user only. The daemon takes requests only from processes of its own user (SO_PEERCRED: root can connect to a socket of mode 0600), in lines of at most MAX_REQUEST (1 MiB): a longer one ends the connection.
  • Never in the way. Clients get only non-blocking writes. One that falls behind by more than MAX_BUFFER is dropped (it can connect again), and a socket that can't be made is logged: the daemon runs on without the live view, whose end doesn't stop it.

The GUI reads the socket with a QLocalSocket, without a thread, and connects again while the daemon runs. Without a daemon it shows what the file would show, and says so.

items.title: Virtual twin
items.text: The preview "In the GUI" runs on a twin per client (runtime/twin.py, Daemon.preview_on_twin()). Twin and Daemon are both a Rig (runtime/rig.py: the Desk, SlotEngine and SlotMixer of a configuration on one surface, and the loop that steps them). The twin's rig is on a Surface(port=NoPort()), an in-memory TwinBackend and a DemoProvider as voice chat. It is built from the Config and the real Names (applications, people, devices, used as stand-ins first) only, so it touches nothing real. Its mode and overrides come from the situation only: the chord, controls and requests change nothing on it (SlotEngine.fixed). slots/world.py turns a Situation into its sound server and people (world()); without a situation the twin runs the world of now by its names (world_of_now()) with the real mode and states (Daemon._situation_now()), and follows them. Its view goes as a separate line {"twin": ...} to its client only (LiveServer.tell_view); Play(event, preview=True) is a hand on it.

items.title: Live preview
items.text:
The GUI can make the daemon run the configuration of its editor before it is saved, and a situation of Simulate, on the device or on a twin of its own (gui/qt/live_preview.py; the daemon's side is Daemon.preview() and Daemon.preview_on_twin()). The design: Previews, in the GUI or on the device.

  • The whole text. StartPreview carries the TOML text the GUI would save (SlotsDocument.render()). The daemon reads it with parse_config(), so the errors are those of check-config, and runs it like a reload: a new mixer on the same surface, sound server and broker, carrying states, overrides and the mode picked over by id. The file is never written. A text with errors, or a changed [mqtt], is answered with the reason, and what runs keeps running. The GUI sends 300 ms after the last edit, and only a document without problems.
  • Where. StartPreview.on_device (true for a GUI of 0.1.0, which knows no other place): on the device, or on the client's twin. Sent again to the other place, the preview moves: the twin ends, or the device runs the file again. KeepPreview and EndPreview cover both.
  • A situation. StartPreview may carry a situation (slots.outcomes.Situation), with or without a config (None: the file's). The SlotEngine runs it in a second Simulation (what_if); see the design for the rest.
  • Replies an old GUI ignores. The daemon answers with lines without version ({"reply": "preview", "ok": ..., "message": ...}), which an older GUI skips like lines of another version. A daemon from before tells no features and ignores requests, so the GUI keeps its preview off.
  • Always back to the file. The preview ends (on the device, and the twin) with EndPreview; when the connection of its client ends; after PREVIEW_TIMEOUT (10 s) without a request (the GUI sends KeepPreview every 3 s, so a window that hangs with its connection open ends it too); and when the file is loaded: on a reload, and when the file changes on disk (checked every second; a twin goes on, it doesn't use the file). A twin also ends when its task fails. The client is told why ({"reply": "ended", ...}). The configuration of the file is kept in memory (Daemon.file_config), so a file that became unusable meanwhile does not keep the preview running.
  • One on the device at a time. A second client takes the device over, and the first one is told: the window someone works in wins over one that was left open, and goes back to its twin. Twins: one per client, no limit.
  • Visible. The status line of systemd ends with "previewing unsaved changes of the GUI", the log tells when a preview starts and ends and why, and the GUI shows a pill.
  • Home Assistant entities survive it. A reload removes the entities of removed channels (an empty retained discovery message, which also deletes them from the entity registry). A preview doesn't: MqttBridge.set_entities(..., preview=True) only stops driving the entities it doesn't have, which stay with their retained states. The next configuration that is no preview removes what it doesn't have; entities only a preview had also lose their retained state, so a preview leaves nothing behind. The mode select gets the modes of the preview.
  • Secrets stay with the user. The text carries the secrets of the file. The GUI sends it only to a daemon of its own user (SO_PEERCRED on its end too), and the runtime directory is the user's own ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, or a directory of mode 0700 in the temporary directory).

items.title: Testing
items.text: The tests run without hardware and without a sound server. just test runs them, just coverage fails below 93 % line and branch coverage, or below 98 % without the Qt widgets (gui/qt).

items.title: What stands in for what
items.text:
Part Tested against The protocol codec, the MIDI parser Captured messages. The raw MIDI device A FIFO. The Surface A recording send, and end to end the SimulatedDevice in memory (tests/support/simulator.py, on the fake clock of the test) and over its socket. The strips, the mixer, the daemon A fake AudioBackend. PulseBackend A fake pulsectl connection. The meters A fake pw-record script. The MQTT bridge, homeassistant strips An in-memory broker (tests/support/mqtt.py): retained messages, subscriptions, last wills, lost connections. The live view A real Unix socket in a short temporary directory: clients that read, that don't read and that go away; requests of the user, of other users and too long ones; the live preview through the daemon. The GUI's live preview A fake live view (a QLocalServer) that answers like the daemon. The Mumble plugin Built with CMake and loaded into a fake Mumble (integrations/mumble/test/fake_mumble.c) that calls its callbacks as a script says, against a real BridgeProvider. Skipped without cmake and a C compiler. The GUI The domain with files in a temporary directory and a fake systemctl; the widgets with pytest-qt on the offscreen platform, a fake sound server, and dialogs the tests answer.

The resolver and the state engine are pure, so each rule of channels, states and slots has unit tests (tests/slots/), and one keeps the table of its example in line with the file.

items.title: Where things go
items.text:
• The tests mirror the packages of the source (tests/config/, tests/strips/, tests/gui/qt/, ...).
  • Fixtures are in the conftest.py files: tests/conftest.py has the guards every test gets (no processes left behind, nothing of the machine touched, no programs started) and the common fakes; the packages have their own (e.g. the window in tests/gui/qt/conftest.py).
  • What tests import, fakes and helpers, is in tests/support/, never in a conftest.py or another test module.

items.title: Design: the form of a channel
items.text: Status: built (2026-11-19), not released; the meter is open (see Open). Builds on Previews of the controls and Output choices.

items.title: Problem
items.text:
The form of a channel works in a wide window and falls apart in a narrower one (about 900 px for the inspector):

  • Choices are a line of fields each: label, device, card, profile, min and max volume, three ▾ buttons and ×. The line is wider than the card, so the whole card scrolls sideways and the help under every option is cut off. The label field shows 5 of the 7 characters the LCD has; the device and card fields show the end of a name.
  • Names (device, card, profile) are a text field with a completer that opens only after typing, and a ▾ menu beside it. Neither says which of the known devices the text matches, and wildcards (bluez_output.*) are a guess.
  • Known devices are only the ones the sound server has now. A device of another profile of the card (the digital output while the card is in its analog profile) and a Bluetooth device that is not connected are missing, although they are what choices are for.
  • Numbers in tables (min_volume, max_volume) are text fields.
  • The labels of choices and profiles go on the LCD, but nothing shows them there: the Display card shows the label of the channel only.
  • Remove is × on lines and a trash can on candidates of the slot cards and in the list.
  • Options that are off by default read as on/off: select and meter are switches, meter_point an empty combo box (unset, it shows nothing instead of the default it takes).
  • What the channel is shows only in its title ("Output"): what a type does (STRIP_TYPE_MEANINGS) shows in the Add menu only. Slots says what a slot is at the top of its form; States has the type as buttons in the middle.

items.title: 1. The top of the form
items.text: Title, id and "Used by" as now, then one sentence of what the type is (STRIP_TYPE_MEANINGS), with "Learn more", like Slots. E.g. "An output device (speakers, headphones): the fader sets its volume. One device, one of several, or whatever is the default output." The cards below then read in that context: the meter of an output shows what plays on it. States gets the same: the type and its sentence at the top, the type buttons move there.

items.title: 2. A form that fits
items.text:
• An option row has its name left of the field (144 px) while the card is wide enough for the name, the field and its help (at least 320 px for the field, option_row.FIELD_WIDTH); below that, the name goes above the field. Help always wraps, nothing in a card is wider than the card.
  • A list of tables (choices, profiles) is a list of small cards, one per entry, not a line of fields:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ⠿  Phones                                           ✎  🗑 │
│    Analog Output (Family 17h HD Audio)                   │
│    needs the card in "Analog Stereo Output"              │
│    20 – 130 %                                            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The label (the default label when there is none), the device by its description, what the choice needs and its volume range, each line only when it says something. ⠿ drags to reorder (Ctrl+Up/Down too): the order is the order Select goes through. ✎ or a double click opens the entry in place as a small form, the same option rows as the rest of the form: Label (as wide as its 7 characters), Device, "Switch the sound card first" (card and profile, folded while unset), Volume (from, to). One entry is open at a time; Esc or a click outside closes it. - Numbers are spin boxes with their unit ("130 %"), empty while unset with the value they take as placeholder ("by default 130 %"); ⟲ unsets them, as on the other options. - The Display card steps through the labels the LCD shows: the channel's, then one step per choice or profile ("Select picked Phones", "Rec picked Digital"), following every key in the form. - Unset options show what they take, from where: "Before the fader (the default of [behavior])". For meter_point that is the empty combo box now. - Remove is the trash can wherever an entry goes (lines, entries, sources, aliases, candidates). × stays on chips, where it takes a word out of a field.

items.title: 3. A field for names
items.text:
One field for every option that names something the sound server or the voice chat has (device, card, profile, match, ignore, person, the aliases), replacing the text field, its completer and its ▾ menu:

  • A click or focus opens the list of what is known; typing filters it (by any part of the name or the description, any case) and keeps it open. Up/Down and Enter pick; Esc closes it and keeps the text.
  • Each entry has two lines: the description, and the name in monospace, with the parts that match the text highlighted in both, and a tag of where it is known from: "default", "now", "profile Digital Stereo", "seen 3 days ago". Presets come first, under their heading, as in the menus now.
  • Under the field, while the text is set: what it matches, with the matches highlighted. "Matches Speaker (Digital Stereo), not there now" or, for bluez_output.*, "Matches 2: WH-1000XM4, Buds Pro (the first one that is there)". "Matches nothing known" in the color of a warning (not an error: a device can come later).
  • Picking a device in a choice that is only known with another profile of its card fills card and profile too.

items.title: 4. Known devices
items.text:
What the field lists, besides what the sound server has now:

  • From the profiles of the cards: each profile of a card that is not active has devices it would make. PipeWire names them from the card and the profile (alsa_card.pci-0000_11_00.4 with output:iec958-stereo gives alsa_output.pci-0000_11_00.4.iec958-stereo), for ALSA cards with the usual profiles; UCM profiles (HiFi) and pro audio name them differently, and get no entry. Tagged "profile ": nothing is stored, it is known as soon as the card is.
  • Remembered: the daemon keeps every device it saw in its state directory (name, description, direction, card, the active profile, when last seen), and sends the list to the GUI with the snapshot. Bluetooth headphones that are off, a USB headset that is unplugged, the digital output after it was used once. Tagged "seen ". A device not seen for 90 days is forgotten; the list has "Forget" on each remembered entry.

items.title: 5. The buttons
items.text:
Select, Rec and Solo of a channel each get a table: what a press does, what a hold does (longer than 0.5 s) and what the LED shows, with the actions of [controls] of the slots (one vocabulary for both):

[channel.main.select]
press = "default"   # make it the default; when it is, the next one (as now)
hold = "next"       # show and control the next device, the default stays
led = "default"

[channel.main.rec]
press = "profile"   # the next profile (as now with profiles)
led = "recording"
Action For Does default output, input Makes the device shown the default; when it is, the next one of device/choices. next output, input The strip shows (and controls) the next one, the default stays. profile output, input The next of profiles. launch apps, auto Starts launch (as now). mute_others all audio While held, the other strips are muted (a solo). talk input While held, Mute is off (push to talk). homeassistant, cycle_modes, mode:<m>, toggle:<s>, { launch = [...] } all As in [controls]. off all Nothing.

The LED takes the indicators of rec and solo now (recording, playing, default, ...), plus shown for next. select = true/false and rec = "recording" (an indicator) keep working as shorthands: the first is press = "default"/"off", the second led. The Buttons card becomes a row per button: what a press does, a hold, the LED; its preview follows the actions.

items.title: 6. The meter
items.text: One choice instead of the switch and the combo box: "Level before the fader" (default), "Level after the fader", "Off", "As in [behavior]". The type sentence at the top (1.) says what the level is of. More than that (a peak hold, a range) only if it turns out to be missing.

items.title: Order
items.text:
1. Built. GUI only: the top of the form, a form that fits, the list of cards with LCDs (and the Display card stepping through the labels of the choices), spin boxes, unset options, trash cans, the meter as one choice (the configuration keeps meter and meter_point).
  2. Built. The field for names, with what the sound server has now and the devices of the profiles (fields/names.py; the matching in domain/sources.py). The matches line is under device, card and profile of a choice; the lists of chips (device of a channel) have the list without it.
  3. Built. Remembered devices (runtime/device_memory.py, a line known_devices of the live view of its own rather than a field of every snapshot, and ForgetDevice).
  4. Built. The buttons (config/buttons.py; VolumeStrip.on_button/act() in strips/base.py, the kinds of strips add do(); mute_others mutes through the binder, the mode actions go to the SlotEngine through StripEnv.actions). Where it differs from 5:
  5. The LED takes press too (what the press does: the default, the profile, the application runs, the mode, held), the default of Select, and of Rec with profiles.
  6. A place in [slots] sets only the LED of a button: what a button does belongs to the channel.
  7. homeassistant sends events for the press and the release (select_pressed, ...); its LED is led, not an entity of Home Assistant. talk, mute_others and homeassistant last while held and take no hold.
  8. On the strips of the chord, Solo does the chord as well as its action.
  9. The GUI: a row per button with three lists (press and hold take typed actions too), the defaults of the type as placeholders; a part set alone keeps the short form (rec = "muted", select = false).

items.title: Decisions (2026-11-19)
items.text:
1. Remembered devices are kept by the daemon: it sees every device, also while no window is open.
  2. A table per button (press, hold, led); the flat options of now stay as shorthands.
  3. All actions of the table above in the first version: default, next, profile, those of [controls], talk, mute_others.
  4. The labels of choices and profiles show in the Display card, a step each; the list of entries has no LCDs.

items.title: Open
items.text: • The meter: is "what it shows" (before/after the fader, off) enough, or should it take more (peak hold, range)?

items.title: Design: output choices
items.text:
Status: built. How to use it: Devices. First designed with strips that moved, which went: History.

One output or input channel switches between several devices, each optionally in its own sound card profile: Phones (analog), Speaker (digital) and Buds (Bluetooth), cycled with Select. Before, that took two or three strips, or Select for the device and Rec for the profile, which did nothing while the Bluetooth device was shown.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
choices is a list of tables ([[channel.out.choices]]; TOML 1.0 has no inline tables over several lines):

Key Required Meaning device yes The node name or description, */? wildcards allowed; with a wildcard, the first device that matches. label no The top line of the LCD while this choice is active; by default the start of the device's description. card with profile The sound card (name or description, wildcards allowed) whose profile the choice needs. profile no The card profile (name or description). Without it, the device is used as it is. min_volume, max_volume no The volume range while this choice is active.

Errors: fewer than 2 choices; choices with device or profiles; profile without card or the other way round; select = false (Select is how one switches). Labels may repeat.

items.title: Behavior
items.text:
• Available: a choice whose device exists, or whose card exists and has its profile (its device appears only after the switch).
  • Active: the choice whose device is the default of its direction; if none is, the one shown last while it is available, else the first available one. A default changed elsewhere (pavucontrol, a Bluetooth connect) is followed when it is one of the choices.
  • Select goes to the next available choice, wrapping around: it switches the card to the choice's profile first (the label shows at once, the device is awaited, and a failed switch goes back), then makes the device the default. A press while a switch is pending goes on from its target, so fast presses step through the choices. A choice shown but not the default is made the default first, like Select on a device channel.
  • A finished default switch ends the pending switch when the command returns, not only when the state shows the new default: a default that the sound server never reports (another program changes it right back) must not pin the strip.
  • The Select LED is on while the active choice's device is the default. Rec keeps its indicator.
  • Label, volume range, fader, Mute, encoder: of the active choice, else of the channel, else of [behavior].
  • Nothing available: like a device channel whose device is missing, absent.
  • Home Assistant: select.<ns>_<id>_output (or _input) with the titles of the choices (label, else device); a second choice of the same title gets a number (Out 2), since the options of a select must differ.
  • list-devices shows the cards with their descriptions and profiles, to fill in card and profile.

items.title: Design: previews of the controls
items.text: Status: built (2026-11-17).

items.title: Problem
items.text: The form of a channel lists its options, with help under each. What they do on the device has to be imagined: which LEDs a rec = "recording" lights and when, how the ring of a balance encoder looks, whether the meter of a pre_fader strip stays up while the fader goes down.

items.title: Idea
items.text:
The form of a channel (and of the pools [pool.apps], [pool.people] and [pool.auto]) groups its options by the part of the strip they are about, in the order of the device from top to bottom, each in a card:

Group Options Preview What it controls device, choices, profiles, match, person, launch, ... none Encoder encoder the encoder with its ring Display label, color, talking_color, lit_when_idle the LCD Buttons rec, solo, select Rec, Solo, Mute, Select Fader and meter fader, min_volume, max_volume, meter, meter_point the meter and the fader Slots absent_after, in_pool, tags none

The card of a part has a small drawing of that part on its left: the same drawing as the window Device (a StripView, cut to the part), so it looks exactly like the device. It shows a short scene, a step at a time like pictures (‹ and ›, with "2 / 4" between them), with a caption under it that says what happens, e.g. for rec = "recording":

  1. "Audio plays": Rec dark.
  2. "An application records": Rec lit.
  3. "Muted": Mute lit.

The scene follows the values in the form at once (also unsaved ones, and the defaults of unset options), and stays at the step shown, so changing an option shows its effect right there. (A first version played the steps in a loop: too fast to follow.)

items.title: Scenes
items.text:
• Encoder (encoder): volume turns the volume up in steps (ring filling, wrap), a push goes back to behavior.reset_volume; balance turns from the center to the right (boost_cut), a push centers it; pick steps through applications (dot), a push pins one (wrap); media seeks forward in a track, a push pauses; homeassistant turns a number.
  • Display: plays (label, volume), the fader moves (the new volume), muted, nothing to control (dark, or lit with lit_when_idle). People: there, talks (talking_color), away.
  • Buttons: plays, records, the default device (output and input only), muted, nothing plays. Each LED lights in the situations its indicator stands for; Mute in the muted one; Select while the device is the default (select).
  • Fader and meter: the fader at the bottom, at the 0 dB mark (with a range across 100 %) and at the top, with the volume of each place (min_volume, max_volume, behavior.unity_at) in the caption; the meter shows a steady level before the fader (pre_fader), or one that follows it (post_fader), and what a mute does to it.

items.title: Parts
items.text:
• gui/domain/demos.py (no Qt): the groups (GROUPS), and scene(part, strip_type, values, behavior), the frames (Frame: a caption and a StripState) from the resolved values. Tested without a window.
  • gui/qt/preview/part_view.py: PartView, a StripView cut to a part with ‹ and › to step through the frames.
  • StripView takes any StripHost (the Preview of the window Device, or a PartView).
  • ChannelsPage builds a card per group.

items.title: Not now
items.text: • Previews in the inspector of the page Slots (the options of a place). The same groups fit there.

items.title: Design: a simulated device
items.text: Status: built (2026-11-17), extended 2026-11-18 (see Decisions).

items.title: Why
items.text:
The X-Touch Extender used for development was defective (the touch sensors of faders 1 and 4 failed) and went back. Without a device nothing above the protocol can be tried outside the tests: no slots on strips, no fader under a finger while a slot changes, no LEDs and texts to look at. The protocol and the behavior of the device are known well (see Hardware, verified on the device on 2026-11-15), so a simulated device can stand in for it: for development, for the GUI, and for tests that run the real Surface end to end.

The model is also how the GUI sees the device (decided 2026-11-17): the daemon keeps one as a mirror of the device it drives, and the GUI shows the mirror. One model of the device, then, for the virtual device, the GUI and the tests.

items.title: Goals
items.text:
• The daemon talks to the simulated device with the same bytes as to the real one. Everything above the transport (Surface, its touch grace, touchless faders, the glide of the motors, the startup sequence, reconnects) runs unchanged, so it gets tried too.
  • The simulated device behaves like the real one where Hardware says how, including faults: a touch sensor that fails (like the returned unit), the device switched off and on (faders move by themselves), unplugged.
  • One model of the device, without IO and without Qt, behind its frontends: the mirror in the daemon (what the GUI shows), a socket server for the daemon, the GUI's drawing to use it, and a test fixture.
  • No root, no kernel modules: it has to work in CI and in a user session.

Not a goal: proving timing-sensitive motor behavior (slow moves, the stop short of the bottom, motor noise). The simulator models the motor simply; those need the real device.

items.title: Rejected: a virtual ALSA MIDI device
items.text: The kernel's snd-virmidi makes raw MIDI devices that Surface would find in /proc/asound/cards without any change. But it needs modprobe (root), its other end is the ALSA sequencer (a second API for the simulator), and it doesn't work in CI. A transport of our own is simpler and testable.

items.title: 1. A transport seam in Surface
items.text:
• hardware/transport.py: a Transport protocol with what Surface uses of RawMidi (write, drain, close, is_open; data and the end come through the callbacks on_data and on_closed). RawMidi is one.
  • A Port finds and opens a transport, LookupError when there is no device:
  • AlsaPort(device_name, proc_asound_cards, dev_snd): finds the card in /proc/asound/cards and opens /dev/snd/midiC<card>D0 as RawMidi.
  • SocketPort(path): connects to the simulator's Unix socket. No simulator running is "not connected", so Surface.run() waits and connects when it starts, and a closed simulator is an unplugged device: the reconnect path gets used.
  • Surface(port=...); the daemon picks the port from the configuration: [device] virtual = true (or xtouch-daemon run --virtual-device, which wins) uses SocketPort(instance.virtual_device_socket_file()), next to the other runtime files ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon/).
  • The log says which: "Connected to the simulated X-Touch-Ext at ...".

items.title: 2. The messages to the device, decoded
items.text:
hardware/protocol.py builds the messages to the device (fader, led, ring, meter, lcd_text, lcd_colors) and decodes those from it. The simulator needs the other direction:

  • decode_host(message) -> HostEvent | None with MotorMoved(strip, value), LedSet(strip, button, Led), RingSet(strip, position, mode, center), MeterSet(strip, level), LcdText(offset, text), LcdColors(colors).
  • And the encoders for what the device sends: fader_moved, fader_touched, button, encoder_turned, encoder_pressed, host_query.
  • Round-trip tests: every encoder against its decoder, both directions, over the full value ranges.

items.title: 3. The model: simulator/device.py
items.text:
SimulatedDevice, pure (no IO, no asyncio, no Qt): it takes bytes from the host and the time, and gives bytes for the host. Time comes in as an argument (now), so tests and frontends drive it.

State per strip:

  • LCD: two lines of 7 characters (written by offset into the 2 x 56 characters, as the device does), and the color.
  • The LEDs of Rec, Solo, Mute and Select: off, on, flashing.
  • The ring: position 0..11, mode, center LED.
  • The meter: the level and when it was set; it falls by itself. The rate of the fall is not measured: about one level per 150 ms, marked as an assumption (see "Fidelity").
  • The fader: where it is (14 bits, but positions in multiples of 4 as the device reports them), the motor's target, touched or not. The motor goes to the target at a fixed speed (about 100 ms over the whole range), not while touched; a motor move sends nothing back (the real device doesn't either).
  • The encoder: pressed or not.

Input (what a hand does), each giving the bytes the device sends:

  • touch(strip, touched), move(strip, fraction): a move while not touched follows the real device: with touch_delay (default 0.07 s) the touch comes after the first moves, as with a quick hand.
  • press(strip, button, pressed), turn(strip, steps), push(strip, pressed).

Faults and events:

  • broken_touch: set[int]: these faders never report a touch (the returned unit: {0, 3}).
  • power_cycle(): sends the host query, then the faders go down by themselves (moves without a touch), as after switching the device on; texts, colors and LEDs are gone until the host sends them again.
  • The host query on connect: F0 00 00 66 15 01 <serial> <challenge> F7 with a made-up serial.
  • Unplugging is the frontends' business (they close the connection).

A changed callback (or a version counter) tells frontends to repaint.

items.title: 4. The mirror: what the GUI shows
items.text:
The Surface keeps a SimulatedDevice as the mirror of the device: every byte it sends goes into it (also while the device is away: then it is what the device will show once it is there), and what the device sends goes in too (observe(): fader moves, touches, encoder pushes). The device's query after switching on changes nothing: the Surface shows everything again on each connect, and after one the mirror doesn't know where the faders are until the motor moved them or the device reported a move (forget_faders()). The live view's strips are the mirror's state (strip_states()), so the GUI shows what reached the device, banners and flashes included, with the motor and the meters moving as the model moves them. The Surface keeps its own record of what each strip shows only where it needs it to send (the strips' values and looks).

What the mirror can't know: what the device does without saying (a motor that stopped short, where the faders are after a connect). It shows what was sent and what the device reported.

items.title: 5. The virtual device and its frontends
items.text:
simulator/server.py: a Unix socket server at instance.virtual_device_socket_file() with one SimulatedDevice. One client at a time (the daemon); a second one is refused, like a device another program has open. A tick (every 10 ms) moves the motors and lets the meters fall. The same device stays when the daemon disconnects and connects again, so a daemon restart sees the faders where they were, as on the real device.

  • CLI: xtouch-daemon virtual-device runs the server headless, logs what the host sets at debug level, and takes a few options (--broken-touch 1,4). (Not simulate: that one simulates slots.)
  • GUI: the GUI can host the server itself (a QLocalServer around the same SimulatedDevice). Then its drawing of the device takes the mouse, sent to the hosted device as a hand:
  • a fader: press = touch, drag = moves, release = let go; Alt-drag moves it without a touch;
  • the buttons: click (press and release), held while the mouse is down;
  • the encoder: the wheel or a drag on the knob turns it (up or right is clockwise), a click pushes it, holding holds it down, and holding on an LED of the ring turns it until the ring lights that LED (gui/qt/preview/encoder_hand.py);
  • a toolbar: plug in / unplug, switch off and on, broken touch per fader.

What it paints still comes from the live view (the daemon's mirror), which is the hosted device's state once it got there; the GUI doesn't paint two models. While the daemon waits for a device that isn't connected, the pill "X-Touch-Ext not connected" offers "Open the virtual device"; nothing starts without a click. - Tests: a fixture that connects a real Surface to a SimulatedDevice through an in-memory transport (no socket), with the loop's clock (looptime). New end-to-end tests: touch grace, touchless faders, the glide arriving, the startup sequence, a power cycle, a reconnect, a slot change under a finger. RecordingSurface stays for the tests that only look at what was sent.

items.title: 6. Fidelity
items.text: What the simulator does is either verified on the device (it says so in Hardware) or an assumption; the assumptions are listed in the module's docstring and in the docs: the speed of the motor, the fall of the meters, the delay of the touch, the moves after switching on. The interactive test is meant to replace assumptions with comparisons on the device.

items.title: Decisions
items.text:
• (2026-11-17) The CLI command is xtouch-daemon virtual-device, the option [device] virtual = true, and xtouch-daemon run --virtual-device overrides it.
  • (2026-11-17) The GUI offers the virtual device but doesn't start it: while the daemon waits for a device that isn't connected, the pill "X-Touch-Ext not connected" has "Open the virtual device". Nothing starts without a click.
  • (2026-11-18) The mouse on the drawing is a hand only in Play; Select (the default) picks and moves slots. Play also works on the device of a running daemon through the live view (live.Play, Surface.play()), so the GUI is a remote control for the real device too. While no daemon runs, "Try without a device" starts one with the virtual device on the file and hosts it: a demo for people without the device. It is the one thing the GUI starts by itself, and only on that click; it ends with the window.

items.title: Design: an interactive device test
items.text: Status: designed (2026-11-18), not built yet. See TODO.md.

items.title: Problem
items.text:
xtouch-daemon test lights everything up once (every LCD in a color, the LEDs, rings and meters, the faders up and down), resets the device and then only prints what happens on it: strip 3: mute pressed, strip 3: encoder +1. The device stays dark meanwhile.

That tells whether the device sends, but not whether it shows what we send it, nor whether the drawing of the GUI (the twin of the device, simulator/device.py and the window Device) shows what the device shows. Both are guesses from the protocol and from looking at the device once; a defective device (touch sensors that don't work, an LED that stays dark) is also only found by chance. And the test needs the daemon stopped, so the GUI can't draw it.

items.title: Decisions (2026-11-18)
items.text:
• It is xtouch-daemon test, extended: the same sweep, then the interactive part below instead of the silence. One test (hardware/selftest.py), started in two ways.
  • The daemon can run it: the GUI starts and ends it with a button (and the command asks a running daemon), the daemon drives the device as always, and the GUI draws it as always (the live view of the mirror of the Surface). So the device and its twin are side by side, input by input, without stopping anything. Without a daemon, xtouch-daemon test opens the device itself, as now.
  • The faders move on request too (the encoder edits them, see below).
  • No inverted LCD lines: tried on the device, it doesn't do them.

items.title: Idea
items.text:
After the sweep, the test doesn't go silent: every strip answers its own controls, so each output of the device is reached by an input on the same strip, and every value of every output can be shown by hand. The log stays as it is, with what the strip shows in answer after each input.

Input on a strip What the strip shows Fader moved The meter shows the position of the fader (0..METER_MAX, sent again while it is up, since the device lets a meter fall by itself). The LCD shows fad 63% for a moment. Fader touched, let go The LCD shows touch / let go for a moment. Rec, Solo, Mute, Select pressed Its LED goes to the next state: off, on, flashing, off. The LCD shows mute on, mute fl, mute off for a moment. Encoder turned Steps the value the encoder edits (see below) up or down, wrapping around, and shows it on the LCD. Encoder pushed Switches what the encoder edits: the position of the ring, its mode, the color of the LCD. The LCD names it.

items.title: The encoder
items.text:
A push switches between four things it edits, the turn steps through all of their values:

  1. ring: the position, 0 (dark) and 1..RING_MAX, in the mode chosen.
  2. mode: the 4 modes of the ring (dot, boost_cut, wrap, spread), each without and with the center LED: 8 values. The position stays, so each mode shows how it lights that position.
  3. color: the 8 backlight colors of the LCD (BLACK .. WHITE).
  4. fader: the motor moves the fader to 0 %, 10 %, ... 100 %, a step a notch, to test the motor and, with a hand on it while it moves, the touch sensor. The meter follows, as for a fader moved by hand.

So every value the protocol can set on the ring, the LCD color and the fader is reached on every strip, and the drawing of the GUI can be compared for each.

items.title: The LCD
items.text:
• Top line: the strip (strip 3) and, after a push of the encoder, what the encoder edits (ring, mode, color, fader).
  • Bottom line: the last input on that strip (mute fl, enc +1, fad 63%, ring 7, cyan), for INPUT_SECONDS (2 s), then back to what the encoder edits and its value.
  • Every strip starts in its own color, as in the sweep, so the colors of the 8 strips can be compared at once.

items.title: What stays
items.text:
• The sweep at the start, unchanged, also when the daemon runs the test.
  • --no-events ends after the sweep, as now.
  • The log of every input (describe()), and the messages the daemon doesn't use (unknown message: ...).
  • Ctrl+C resets the device and ends.

items.title: The daemon runs the test
items.text:
• Requests (live/messages.py), as for the preview: StartTest, KeepTest (the GUI sends it while the mode runs) and EndTest; the snapshot says test: bool. Only a GUI of the same user (owned), as for Play and Try.
  • While it runs, the Desk gives the events of the device to the test bench instead of the slots; the slots, states and Home Assistant go on as usual (the entities still tell what the slots would show), but nothing of theirs reaches the device. A control of Home Assistant that would act on the device waits.
  • It ends with EndTest, when the connection of its GUI closes, after TEST_TIMEOUT without a request (like PREVIEW_TIMEOUT), and when the device goes away or is switched (Surface.use). Then the daemon draws everything of the slots again, as after a preview or a device that came back.
  • A preview and the test don't run at the same time: starting one ends the other.
  • The GUI: a "Test the device" button next to Play and Preview, checked while the mode runs, with a bar that says what each control does (the table above). Play works during the test: a click on the drawing is an input the test bench answers, the same as one on the device; so does the virtual device the GUI hosts.
  • The command: xtouch-daemon test with a daemon running asks the daemon for the mode (and ends it with Ctrl+C) instead of failing because the device is taken; without a daemon it opens the device itself, as now, and the GUI can't draw it.

items.title: Building it
items.text:
• hardware/selftest.py: run_selftest grows the interactive part, a TestBench on a Surface, used by the command and by the daemon (the sweep too). It takes the events of the device and keeps the state of each strip in a typed dataclass (LED states, what the encoder edits, ring position and mode, color, fader). A temporary text ends with a timer per strip, which the next input on that strip replaces; the old handle is cleared before anything awaits, so two quick inputs can't leave a timer running. A task sends the meters of raised faders again.
  • runtime/daemon.py: the mode (start, keep, end, timeout), the Desk handing over to the bench and back, drawing the slots again at the end.
  • live/: the requests and Snapshot.test; gui/qt/window/device_view.py: the button and the bar.
  • cli/daemon.py: test asks a running daemon (system.instance) first.
  • Tests: the bench against the simulated device (tests/support/simulator.py, MemoryPort): an input as the device sends it, then what the mirror shows (LED states, ring, color, fader, LCD texts, meter), and that a temporary text goes back; the mode of the daemon (start, the slots not reaching the device, the ends, drawing again); the GUI's button and bar.
  • Docs: guides/gui.md (the button), reference/commands.md#test (what each input does, a running daemon), reference/hardware.md (testing a device).

items.title: Design: launching applications
items.text:
Status: built. How to use it: Applications and People.

The idea: the Select button of a strip whose application is not there starts it. A "VoIP" strip starts Mumble and connects it to the server, a "Music" strip starts the music player.

items.title: Where it goes
items.text:
Where launch An apps channel Select launches while none of its applications runs. [controls] of a slot: select = { launch = [...] } Select of that slot launches, whatever the slot shows, while its when holds. This is how the voice chat starts: 7 = { select = { launch = ["mumble", "mumble://..."] }, when = "not call" } on the slot VoIP shows on in a call. output, input channels Not allowed: Select makes the device the default. homeassistant channels Not allowed: Home Assistant owns the strip and must never send a command. person channels, [pool.people], places Not allowed: a launch is a control of the slot.
  • launch: the program, then its arguments, as a list; not empty, and no part empty.
  • A single string is accepted too and split with shlex.split (quotes like a shell, nothing expanded: no ~, $VAR, globs, pipes or &&). A command line is what people copy from a .desktop file or a terminal; the GUI's chips stay the canonical form (it saves a list). The split happens at validation, so check-config and the GUI show the parts.
  • launch_when_running: Select starts the command also while the application runs. For Mumble that is useful: a running Mumble takes the URL and connects, and mumble without a URL brings its window to the front.

items.title: Mumble URLs
items.text:
From the Mumble documentation:

mumble://[username[:password]@]<address>[:port]/[channelpath][?title=<servername>][&url=<serverurl>]
  • The port defaults to 64738. Special characters of the channel path must be URL-encoded (Gaming%20Night). Subchannels are separated by /. When the channel can't be reached, Mumble stays in the default channel.
  • ?version=1.2.0 was needed only before Mumble 1.2.4. title and url matter only when the link is dropped into the server browser.
  • A password in the URL ends up in the configuration file and in the process list (/proc/*/cmdline is readable by every user). Leave it out and let Mumble remember it, or use a certificate.

A running Mumble accepts the URL too: on Linux, Mumble's main.cpp hands the URL of a second instance over D-Bus (openUrl on info.mumble.mumble, then the legacy net.sourceforge.mumble.mumble) to the running one and exits; without a URL it asks the running one to focus. Only --multiple starts a second client. Verified in the source (src/mumble/main.cpp), not with a real Mumble.

items.title: When an application "runs"
items.text:
Select launches only while the application doesn't run:

  • An apps channel runs while a stream matches match, a process whose name contains one of the match entries runs, or the program of launch runs. So a silent Mumble (no stream) counts.

  • A control runs while the program of its launch runs.

  • Processes are matched like the processes of states (system/processes.py): the kernel's comm and the file name of the program, in lower case, containing the pattern. They are read every 2 s (binder.PROCESS_INTERVAL) while anything needs them.

  • The program of launch is the file name of its first part, matched exactly: flatpak must not match flatpak-portal, which runs all the time. For ["flatpak", "run", "info.mumble.Mumble"] that is useless (the program is flatpak), so name the application in match.
  • A match entry like signal also counts unrelated processes whose name contains it. The cost is a Select that does nothing; list-apps and ps -e show what runs.

items.title: Starting it
items.text:
• Never through a shell. The list goes to exec as it is.
  • Detached from the daemon's service. With a systemd user manager (its socket $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/systemd/private) and systemd-run in PATH: systemd-run --user --quiet --collect --unit=xtouch-launch-<program>-<random> --property=WorkingDirectory=~ -- argv…. Otherwise a plain process in a session of its own (start_new_session), stdin/stdout/stderr on /dev/null, waited for by a thread so it does not stay a zombie.
  • Deviation from the first idea, systemd-run --scope: a scope runs the command as a child of systemd-run, which is a child of the daemon, with the daemon's environment. The daemon's service starts with default.target, often before the desktop imports WAYLAND_DISPLAY/DISPLAY into the user manager, so a GUI application started from a scope may find no display. A transient service gets the user manager's environment of the moment, is not a child of the daemon (no zombie, survives a restart of the daemon without question), and its output goes to the journal (journalctl --user -u 'xtouch-launch-*'). --collect removes the unit also when it failed.
  • Logging: every start is logged (info, with the command), a program that is not in PATH is a warning (checked before, with shutil.which, so systemd-run does not fail later in the background), an OSError of the start a warning, an exit of the started process with an error code (fallback mode, or systemd-run itself) a warning. A launch that does not show up in 15 s is a warning. Nothing of it stops the daemon.
  • Debounce: no second launch within 5 s (LAUNCH_DEBOUNCE) of the last one while the application is not up yet, so a double press starts it once.
  • Reload: the launch state belongs to the strip or control and starts anew with a reload; the started application is not affected.

items.title: The Select LED
items.text: It flashes while launching (until the application runs, at most 15 s, LAUNCH_TIMEOUT), is on while it runs, and off otherwise; without launch it stays off. The device flashes the LED itself (Mackie Control Led.FLASH); the daemon sends it once.

items.title: Security
items.text:
• Commands come only from the configuration: the file, or the configuration of a live preview. The live view only accepts clients of the same user (SO_PEERCRED in live.py), who could edit the file anyway. A preview whose launch runs something is no more than that user can do in a shell.
  • Home Assistant and MQTT can never send a command: nothing arriving over MQTT reaches launch, and homeassistant channels can't have it.
  • No Home Assistant button entity for now. A button per launch that runs the configured command would be safe (it runs only the configured command, never one from MQTT), but it lets anyone who can press buttons in Home Assistant start programs on the desktop, also while nobody sits there. Left out until there is a use for it.

items.title: Later
items.text:
• Focus the window when Select is pressed while the application runs. On Wayland there is no portable way (KWin scripts, GNOME extensions, the Sway/Hyprland IPC differ, see Layouts). For Mumble, launch_when_running with launch = ["mumble"] already does it through Mumble's own D-Bus focus.
  • A launch_process option for commands whose program is not the application (flatpak run, gtk-launch), if match turns out not to be enough.
  • A Home Assistant button (see Security).

items.title: Design: presets
items.text:
Status: built. How to use it: Presets.

The idea: common groups of applications (every browser, every voice chat, every game started from Steam) get a name, so nobody has to look up what each application calls its streams and processes. match = ["@browsers"] instead of match = ["brave", "firefox", "chromium", ...].

items.title: Where applications are matched by name
items.text:
Where Matched against Kind match of apps channels the application name (application.name) and binary (application.process.binary) of each stream streams apps and recording of states the same streams exclude of [pool.apps] (what apps and auto never take) the same streams processes of states the names of the processes (comm, and the file name of the program) processes "runs" of an apps channel with launch the processes, with the match entries processes the program of launch the processes, the file name of the program exactly none: a command, not a list of names person of person channels, [aliases] names of people, exact names of applications none

Presets go where the user writes a list of parts of names: the first four rows. The fifth follows from match.

items.title: How a preset is written
items.text:
• @name in the list, next to plain names: match = ["@voip", "my-voice-app"]. An @ never starts the name of an application or process in practice, and TOML needs no quoting beyond the string. A separate option (match_presets = [...]) was the alternative; one list is shorter and works the same in every list.
  • Names are lower case with hyphens: @steam-games.

items.title: What a preset stands for
items.text:
presets.py holds the table: each Preset has a description, the names for lists of streams (streams) and for lists of processes (processes), either of which may be None (not for that kind of list), and a note for the docs.

  • The names are matched like the user's: as parts of the name, ignoring case. A preset is nothing but a list of names, so it can't do anything the user could not write, and list-apps and check-config explain it in the same terms. Exact matching or regular expressions would be a second matching mode for little gain.
  • A preset stands for different names in each kind of list. Streams and processes are named differently: a Proton game plays as Planet Crafter.exe (binary wine64-preloader), but its processes are Wine's, and .exe in a list of processes matches Wine's helpers (explorer.exe, services.exe) and Proton's steam.exe. Steam starts every game through its reaper, which is the reliable process, and has no stream.
  • Errors at validation. An unknown preset lists the known ones. A preset in a list it has no names for says where it can be used. Both are pydantic errors of the option, so check-config and the GUI show them at their place (channel.browser.match: ...).

items.title: Expanded when the configuration is validated
items.text:
The models expand presets in a validator of the list's type (StreamNames in config/names.py, Streams and Processes in slots/model.py), so the strips, the states, the pools and list-apps see plain names. The Presets metadata of the type marks the option for the GUI's schema.

The entries as written stay on the model (_WithPresets.written(), a private attribute filled by a wrap validator), for what explains the configuration to people: check-config shows @browsers (firefox, librewolf, ...). The GUI edits the TOML document itself, not the models, so it always shows @browsers and writes it back as it was.

An apps channel with launch counts its applications as running when a process of theirs runs: before presets, the match entries were matched against the processes as they are. Now the plain entries still are, and each preset counts with its names for processes (AppsStripConfig.process_names), so @steam-games counts reaper, not .exe.

items.title: The presets
items.text:
Each is a short list of well-known applications, checked against what they report on a real system where possible (Brave, Mumble and a Proton game on this machine) and against their packages otherwise. Choices:

  • No broad names. steam (the client runs all the time), .exe in processes, chrome in processes (every Electron application runs a chrome_crashpad_handler), element (elementary OS's io.elementary.*), bare zen, jellyfin (the server is a process too), dragon (games). Tests list such names for each preset and fail if one matches them.
