  • Streams can't tell who started a game. A Proton game from Steam and a Wine game from Lutris play alike, so the streams of @steam-games and @games are the same: every Windows program under Wine.
  • @games processes: reaper and wineserver. Lutris and Heroic leave no process of their own while a game runs (Lutris's lutris-wrapper names itself only with an optional Python module), so there is no reliable marker for them. wineserver runs while any Windows program runs under Wine or Proton, which on a desktop is mostly games, and a few seconds after it (which the delay_off of a mode covers anyway). Native games from Lutris or Heroic are not part of it.
  • Electron. Before Electron 40 every Electron application names its streams "Chromium" (with its own binary), so chromium in @browsers also takes their sounds, e.g. Discord's notifications. Leaving Chromium out of a browser preset would be worse; the docs say it.
  • REAPER. The digital audio workstation's process is reaper too, so @steam-games in processes also matches while it runs. Its users name their games in processes instead; the note of the preset says so.

The docs page lists every preset with its names; a test checks that its table is presets.markdown_table(), so it can't go stale.

items.title: Where presets show
items.text:
• check-config: each preset with what it stands for, in channels and states.
  • list-apps: the presets each application that plays is part of (Brave (@browsers)), to find the right one.
  • The GUI: the options with the Presets metadata suggest the presets of their kind first (a "Presets" section of the menu, the description beside each, what it stands for as the tooltip), then the names of the sound server; a processes list, which had no suggestions, gets the presets for processes. The chip of a preset is outlined instead of filled and has the same tooltip.

items.title: Design: previews, in the GUI or on the device
items.text: Status: built (2026-11-19). It replaces Try changes and situations and The virtual twin.

items.title: Problem
items.text:
Two features of the GUI show something that isn't real yet, and both grew a way to show it:

  • Unsaved edits of the configuration reach the device with "Try on the device" (StartPreview).
  • Simulate shows another situation. It reaches the device with "Try on the device" too, and otherwise runs on a virtual twin in the daemon (StartTwin).

So edits can only be tried on the device, Simulate in both places, and two protocols with their own heartbeat, timeout and ending do the same thing for different targets. On top of that, four things all looked like "the device" in the discussion: the real device, the SimulatedDevice, the twin and the drawing. This design names each of them once and puts both features behind one preview with one control: where the preview shows.

items.title: Terms
items.text:
One word for one thing, in the code, the docs and here.

Term What it is Where device The X-Touch Extender the daemon drives. It is the real one over USB MIDI, or the virtual device. Below, "the device" means either. hardware/ virtual device A device model behind a Unix socket, started by xtouch-daemon virtual-device or by the GUI ("Try without a device"). The daemon speaks the same MIDI bytes to it as to the real one (SocketPort). simulator/server.py, gui/qt/virtual_device.py device model SimulatedDevice: what a device shows (LCD texts and colors, LEDs, rings, meters, faders, touches), pure Python, without IO or Qt. It is the one model of a device. simulator/device.py mirror The device model in each Surface, fed with every byte the surface sends and receives. It shows what the device shows, or will show once it is connected. Surface.mirror rig The strips of a configuration on one surface: the hands on them (Desk), the slots (SlotEngine), the controllers (SlotMixer) and the loop that steps them. runtime/rig.py twin A second rig in the daemon, one per GUI window that asks for it. Its surface has no device, and its sound server and voice chat are made up. Its mirror is all there is of it. runtime/twin.py drawing What the window Device of the GUI paints: always a mirror that the daemon sends, of the device or of the window's twin. gui/qt/window/device_view.py preview What a window shows that isn't real yet: its unsaved edits, with the situation of Simulate while it is open. Simulate always includes the edits. situation A what-if of Simulate: the mode, the states on, the channels and pools present, and how many people, applications and devices. slots.outcomes.Situation 
flowchart LR
    subgraph Daemon
        direction TB
        Rig[the daemon's rig] --> Surface --> Mirror[mirror]
        Twin[a twin per window] --> TSurface[surface, no device] --> TMirror[mirror]
    end
    Surface -- MIDI --> Device[device: real, or virtual]
    Mirror -- "Snapshot (every window)" --> Drawing
    TMirror -- "view (its window only)" --> Drawing[drawing of a window]

items.title: Rules
items.text:
1. The drawing is a device preview first. It can always mirror what the device shows right now.
  2. The daemon drives everything that is drawn. The GUI computes no strips. The drawing is a mirror of the device or of the window's twin. Without a daemon, the strips are dark and the GUI says how to start the daemon.
  3. One model of a device. The virtual device, every mirror and the tests use the device model.
  4. One rig, two uses. The daemon's strips and a twin are both a Rig, so they behave the same: steps, delays, banners, controllers, meters.
  5. One preview per window: the editor's configuration, in the situation of Simulate while it is open.
  6. One control decides where the preview shows, for the edits and Simulate alike. "In the GUI" is the default. "On the device" is the user's approval that the device changes before the configuration is saved.
  7. Home Assistant never sees a preview. Its entities show the file and the real situation.

items.title: Where the preview shows
items.text:
The control "Preview" sits next to Save and apply, while the window has a preview (unsaved edits, or Simulate open). It has three positions:

Position The device runs A twin runs The drawing shows Meant for In the GUI (the default) The file, in reality The preview The twin Seeing the edits and Simulate without touching the device. On the device The preview Nothing The device, which shows the preview Trying it for real: an intentional choice, the device changes before a save. Off The file, in reality Nothing The device, as it is A user who can't see the device and wants to see what it shows. Rarely used.
  • Without a preview (no edits, Simulate closed) the control is gone. The device runs the file, and the drawing mirrors it: there is nothing else to show.
  • A new window starts with "In the GUI". The position stays as it is set until the window closes.
  • Simulate opened while "Off" moves the control to "In the GUI"; closing Simulate (Esc) moves it back to "Off".
  • The cards of the page Slots (what a slot shows, why, who waits) are the slots of what the drawing shows.
  • Play acts on what the drawing shows: the twin's strips, or the device's.
  • The configuration of the preview is the editor's document. The twin needs no daemon that reads this file; "On the device" needs one, as now.

items.title: The situation of a twin
items.text:
• Simulate open: the situation of Simulate.
  • Simulate closed (only edits): the situation of now. The daemon takes it from its real slots at every step: the mode, the states that are on, the channels present, and how many people, applications and devices. So the twin shows what the device would show with the edits right now, and follows when reality changes. A state or channel that only the edits have starts as Simulate would start it (off, present).

Either way its sound server is made up: the twin touches nothing real (see The twin).

items.title: Changing the position
items.text:
• To "On the device": the daemon runs the preview on the device (as StartPreview does now). The window's twin ends, and the drawing shows the device.
  • From "On the device": the device goes back to the file and the real situation.
  • To "In the GUI": a twin starts with the preview, and the drawing shows it.
  • To "Off": the twin ends, and the drawing shows the device.
  • Another window chooses "On the device": the device runs that window's preview. The first window is told, and goes back to "In the GUI".

items.title: How a preview ends
items.text:
• Save and apply: the daemon loads the file. The edits are no preview any more. If Simulate is open, its situation stays a preview where the control says.
  • Revert, and Simulate closed (Esc): nothing is left to preview. The control is gone, the twin ends, and the device runs the file again.
  • The window closes or stops answering (PREVIEW_TIMEOUT, 10 s): the daemon ends its twin and, if the window had the device, runs the file on it again.
  • The file changes on disk, or the daemon is reloaded: someone acted on the file on purpose, so the device runs it. A window that had the device is told why and goes back to "In the GUI". A twin keeps running the window's document.
  • The daemon stops or restarts: the window loses its preview. Once a daemon is there again, the window asks again where its control says.

items.title: Without a device, without a daemon
items.text:
• A daemon, no device connected: every position works. On the device, the mirror shows what the device will show once it is connected, and the bar above the drawing says it isn't.
  • No daemon: no preview, no Simulate, no drawing. The control and Simulate are off and say how to start the daemon (xtouch-daemon install-service --now), or offer "Try without a device".

items.title: The twin
items.text:
A twin is a Rig built from a configuration and a situation, and from nothing of the daemon. It gets no reference to the real sound server, surface, bridge, voice chat, media players or state directory. That is the guarantee, not a check at each effect.

Real In a twin AudioBackend (the sound server) TwinBackend: an AudioState in memory. Commands change it and report it, like the sound server does. AudioState Made from the situation (slots/world.py). The real one is never passed on. Voice chat provider DemoProvider with the people of the situation. Meters (pw-record per target) A made-up signal, fed through the same Meter, scaled by the gain of the target. launch A launcher that starts nothing. MQTT, Home Assistant, media players None. state_dir (choices, people) None: no file is read or written. The device A Surface on NoPort: a port that is never there. The surface writes everything into its mirror anyway. Mode and overrides The situation's only. The chord, the controls and requests of modes and overrides change nothing (SlotEngine.fixed). Log xtouch_daemon.twin.

items.title: The world of a situation
items.text:
world(scene, situation, names) makes the twin's sound server and voice chat:

Part of the scene In the world, unless the situation removed it output / input channel A device for each of its devices (a wildcard gets one that matches it), or the default one without devices. apps channel A stream that its first match entry takes. person channel That person in the voice chat. homeassistant channel Nothing: it is always present. apps, people, devices pool As many as the situation says: the real ones first, then made up (App 1, Alice, Device 1). Pools of channels Their channels, as channels are. Pools of your own One stand-in that the pool takes, while the situation has it present.

items.title: Real names first
items.text:
The stand-ins of the pools take the names of what is real right now first: the applications that play, the people in the voice chat, the devices without a channel. They are plain strings, copied: the twin has no audio behind them. The device does the same with a situation, and there it has audio behind them.

The daemon gives a twin new names when they change. So the strips of a twin follow reality: a stand-in "Spotify" becomes "App 1" when Spotify stops playing. Its volume on the twin starts again at 100 %. That is accepted (decision 4).

items.title: The protocol
items.text:
One preview per client replaces StartPreview/StartTwin, KeepPreview/KeepTwin and EndPreview/EndTwin:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class StartPreview:
    """
    Run `config` (None: the file's) in `situation` (None: the situation of now) on the device or on a twin of this
    client; sent again, it follows. "Off" sends `EndPreview`.
    """

    config: str | None
    situation: Situation | None
    on_device: bool


class KeepPreview: ...  # the heartbeat, every 3 s


class EndPreview: ...  # nothing to preview any more


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Play:
    event: StripEvent
    preview: bool = False  # on the window's twin, not on the device
  • Replies: Reply("preview", ok, message) to StartPreview, with the errors of the configuration. Reply("ended", True, why) when the daemon ended the preview (another window took the device, the file changed, a missed heartbeat, the twin failed, the daemon stops). A window that lost its daemon (the connection ended) asks again with its next heartbeat.
  • The twin's view is a line of its own, {"twin": TwinView} (a snapshot has a field preview already), sent to its window only while it changes. On the device, the snapshot shows the preview as before (preview, simulated).
  • A feature on_device in FEATURES tells the new StartPreview. A daemon without it is too old for the GUI's preview, and the GUI says to restart it.
  • Only the user's own clients (peer_uid), as now: the configuration may hold secrets.

items.title: The GUI
items.text:
• The control "Preview" next to Save and apply: "In the GUI", "On the device", "Off", while there is a preview. It replaces the switch "Try on the device" and the bar "Only in the drawing". Each position has a tooltip that says what the device and the drawing show.
  • The pill next to it says where the preview shows and what it is: "In the GUI, not saved", "On the device · simulated", "Off: the device runs the file", "Sending…", "Paused: problems".
  • The bar above the drawing says what the drawing shows: "Preview in the GUI", or the device's own text with "· preview" while it runs the preview (e.g. "Live · preview"). Until the twin's first view arrives, the drawing shows the device.
  • The state bar of Slots always shows the device's states: its overrides change the device, not the preview. The cards and the why-panel show the twin while the drawing does.
  • Simulate needs a daemon of this user, as now. Esc ends it.
  • Edits reach the preview a moment after each change (debounced, as now). A document with problems is not sent: the preview keeps the last one that was.

items.title: Decisions (2026-11-19)
items.text:
1. The drawing is a device preview first: "Off" always shows the device as it is.
  2. One control for edits and Simulate, with three positions: "In the GUI", "On the device", "Off". Simulate always includes the edits and shows where they show.
  3. "In the GUI" is the default. "On the device" is an intentional choice: the user approves that the device changes before a save. "Off" is for a user who can't see the device.
  4. Simulate opened while "Off" moves to "In the GUI", and back when it closes.
  5. One rig for the device and the twins (Rig). A twin's mode and states are the situation's only.
  6. Real names first on the twin, following reality. Its strips may change while the situation stays.
  7. Simulate needs a daemon. There is no rig in the GUI.
  8. One twin per window, no limit. The device takes one window's preview at a time.

items.title: What changed from what was built before
items.text:
1. Protocol: one StartPreview with on_device, Play(preview=...); the twin messages go. The daemon's preview and twins become one session per client.
  2. Daemon: a twin with no situation runs the situation of now (Daemon._situation_now(): the real mode and states, world_of_now() with the real names), and follows it.
  3. GUI: the control "Preview" ("In the GUI" by default); edits preview on the twin; the drawing, cards and Play follow the control; the pill's and the bar's texts.
  4. Docs: the GUI guide (Preview, Simulate), the architecture of the live view, the changelog; the two designs it replaces moved to history/.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
• Where: for each position, with edits, with Simulate and with both: what the device runs, whether a twin runs, and what the window is sent.
  • Changing the position: each change ends or starts what it should; a second window takes the device, and the first one goes back to "In the GUI"; Simulate opened while "Off" moves to "In the GUI" and back.
  • The situation of now: a twin without Simulate follows a change of the real states and members.
  • Inertness: a twin with Play and a reconfigure calls nothing real; the real strips and slots stay as they are.
  • Ending: Save, Revert and Esc, the window gone, a missed heartbeat, a failed twin, the file changed, the daemon restarted.
  • GUI: with a fake daemon, the control sends what it should; the drawing, the cards and Play follow it; without a daemon, the guidance.

items.title: Not in this design
items.text: • The GUI doesn't notice when the file changes on disk. A Save then overwrites a change the user never saw. A file watcher with "The file changed on disk: Load it / Keep my changes" is needed with or without previews; it gets a design of its own.

items.title: Design: the voice chat
items.text:
Status: built. How to use it: People and Mumble; the protocol of the bridge: The voice chat bridge. First designed with the layouts.

The wish: a strip per participant of the voice chat, with their level on the meter and their volume on the fader.

items.title: Can a mixer see the participants?
items.text:
Not through PipeWire. Mumble, TeamSpeak and Discord mix every participant into one playback stream, so pw-dump shows one node per client, never one per participant. The participants are only known inside the client.

Client Participants and talking Local volume per participant From outside on Linux Mumble (1.5) Plugin API: getUsersInChannel, getUserName, mumble_onUserTalkingStateChanged, onUserAdded/Removed Not in the API (requestLocalMute/isUserLocallyMuted mute only). But mumble_onAudioSourceFetched(pcm, …, isSpeech, userID) gets each participant's audio before the mix, may change it (a plugin can apply its own gain) and can measure its peak. The built-in local volume (since 1.3) is not reachable. (MumblePlugin.h) D-Bus net.sourceforge.mumble.mumble: getTalkingUsers, getCurrentUrl, self mute/deaf, transmit mode (DBus.h); mumble rpc the same few commands (RPC docs). No participant list, no per-user volume. Server side (Ice): users and channels, but no talking state and no client-local volume. TeamSpeak 3 ClientQuery (local TCP 25639, API key): clientlist, notifytalkstatuschange, notifycliententerview (client query library) Plugin SDK only: setClientVolumeModifier(connection, client, dB), and the client stores it (forum). No ClientQuery command for it was found. ClientQuery is reachable from another process. TeamSpeak ⅚ has no stable public API (not re-checked). Discord Local RPC (Unix socket discord-ipc-N): GET_SELECTED_VOICE_CHANNEL, SPEAKING_START/STOP events SET_USER_VOICE_SETTINGS (volume 0..200, mute) (Userdoccers) The rpc* scopes are for "approved partners" only (Discord OAuth2); projects use Discord's own StreamKit client id and token endpoint instead, without refresh tokens, and Discord restores the volumes when the app disconnects (Noctalia Discord Voice). Fragile and a ToS gray area.

So per-participant levels need code inside the client (a Mumble plugin, a TeamSpeak plugin). Per-participant volume needs the same (Mumble: the plugin applies its own gain in onAudioSourceFetched; TeamSpeak: setClientVolumeModifier), or Discord's restricted RPC. Participant lists and talking states alone are possible from outside for TeamSpeak (ClientQuery) and Discord (RPC), not for Mumble.

items.title: A provider, and a bridge
items.text:
graph LR
    Mumble[Mumble + plugin] -- "JSON lines" --> Bridge
    Bridge[BridgeProvider<br/>$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon-voip.sock] --> Strips[strips of people]
    Demo[DemoProvider] --> Strips
    Later[later: TeamSpeak, Discord] -.-> Strips
  • VoipProvider (voip/provider.py): a snapshot of Participants (id, name, talking, muted, volume, level), connected, an on_change callback, set_volume(), set_muted(), run(), and what it can do (capabilities: volume, mute, levels). The strips show only what the provider can do.
  • BridgeProvider: the daemon serves a Unix socket; a plugin inside the client connects, sends the participants as JSON lines and gets the commands back. The protocol is the same for every client, so the daemon needs no client libraries. To try it by hand: socat - UNIX-CONNECT:$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon-voip.sock and a pasted line.
  • DemoProvider: participants from the configuration, with volume and mute kept in memory and a talking pattern.
  • Volume and mute while away. The Mumble plugin keeps them per session (one who comes back gets a new session at 100 %), and the bridge has no notion of names. So the provider remembers what the strips set by the participant's name (ignoring case) and sends it again when someone of that name appears. A mute changed in the client replaces the kept one, so coming back does not undo it. It lasts while the daemon runs; the provider survives reloads (not a changed [voip]).
  • Later: TeamSpeak (plugin SDK, or ClientQuery without volume); Discord only if the RPC scopes open up; remembering the volumes across restarts.

items.title: The Mumble plugin: mute and threads
items.text:
Mute on a voip strip is Mumble's own local mute (requestLocalMute, isUserLocallyMuted of plugin API 1.0), so Mumble shows it and a mute set in Mumble lights the button. The first version had its own mute (gain 0 in mumble_onAudioSourceFetched), because the local mute needs API calls the plugin had no safe place for:

  • Mumble calls the event callbacks in its main thread, and runs every API function there: called from another thread, it is queued to the main thread and the caller waits (Mumble's docs/dev/plugins/MumbleAPI.md, "Multithreading"). A callback that waits for a thread that waits for an API call would wait for itself, and the plugin's mumble_shutdown has to wait for its threads before Mumble unloads the library.
  • No callback comes regularly in the main thread. The talking states come only while someone talks, the users' callbacks only when someone comes or goes; a request of the daemon can wait for neither. The only timers that call plugins are those of positional audio (mumble_initPositionalData every second while no positional plugin is linked), which would make the plugin a positional one in Mumble's settings: rejected.
  • Mumble bounds the wait: a call that doesn't get to run within 800 ms is cancelled and fails with MUMBLE_EC_API_REQUEST_TIMEOUT (C_WRAPPER in src/mumble/API_v_1_x_x.cpp, the same in every release with plugin API 1.0: 1.4.230 to 1.6.870).

So the plugin has two threads: the socket thread never calls the API and only queues the mute requests (a counter per participant); the "Mumble thread" makes the requests and reads the local mute of the participants every 500 ms while the daemon is connected (Mumble has no event for it; the callbacks read it too when they refresh the users). No thread holds the plugin's lock during an API call, so a callback never waits for one. Only mumble_shutdown does: it drops the requests that have not started and waits for a call under way, which can't run then and fails after the 800 ms; the thread makes no call after that. Shutting down takes those 800 ms only if a call was under way at that moment.

While a request is under way the plugin reports the requested mute; when Mumble refuses one, it logs why (api.log) and reports Mumble's mute again, so the button goes back. A locally muted participant who talks has the talking state MUMBLE_TS_TALKING_MUTED, which counts as talking: the backlight shows it, as with the first version's mute. Their level is 0: Mumble does not mix them and fetches none of their audio.

Others' self-mute and deafen are not in the API. Plugin API 1.0 has no function for them (isLocalUserMuted and isLocalUserDeafened are the user's own), getUserComment is the free text of the user, and the talking state MUMBLE_TS_TALKING_MUTED of another user means the local mute: AudioOutputSpeech.cpp sets MutedTalking only for bLocalMute (since 1.6 also for a local volume of 0), while ClientUser::setSelfMute/setSelfDeaf emit muteDeafStateChanged, which the plugin manager doesn't forward (it connects talkingStateChanged only). Someone who muted themselves sends no audio, so they are just passive.

items.title: Design: channels, states and slots
items.text:
Status: built (0.1.0). How to use it: Channels, states and slots. How it came to be, with the reviews and the live test: History.

The pages of this design:

  • this one: the model, the names, the conditions, an example;
  • Channels and pools: what a strip controls, and which one of several;
  • States and modes: when something matters;
  • Slots: where it shows, the resolver, the controls of a slot;
  • Where the people sit: the pools people, apps and auto, with use cases;
  • Pools of your own: proposed, pools of applications and of people that the user defines;
  • In the daemon: the runtime, Home Assistant, the commands, the GUI.

items.title: Why
items.text:
A [[strip]] of the old format answered four questions at once, spread over several mechanisms:

Question Old format What does it control? type and its options. When does it matter? Implicitly, collapse, the rules of a [[layout]]. How is it related to other strips? inherit (by layout and position), the group of voip strips. Where is it on the device? Its position in a list, shifted by collapse, replaced as a whole by a layout.

That made simple wishes hard: "VoIP and the Mic only during a call, else auto there" needed a group that collapses together; a strip that matters while gaming and while calling needed two layouts that can't both be active; inherit referred to "strip 6 of the layout default", so moving a strip changed its meaning; collapse moved every strip after it, which hurts muscle memory.

items.title: The model
items.text:
Each concept answers one question and is edited in one place.

Concept Answers Edited on Channel What a strip controls: a device, applications, a person in the voice chat, a Home Assistant strip. Channels Pool Which one of several a strip takes: whatever plays and has no slot, the people in the voice chat, the next present channel of a list. Channels State When something matters: a named on/off condition, live, with a manual override. A mode is a state that excludes the other modes. States Slot Where: one of the 8 strips of the device, with a stack of candidates (channels or pools, each with a condition). Slots Controls What a fader, encoder or button of a slot does whatever the slot shows (a Home Assistant knob, starting Mumble). Slots

items.title: Names
items.text:
Channels, pools, states and the ids of controls share one namespace: lower case letters, digits and _, unique across all four (a control id names Home Assistant entities like a channel id does).

  • Built in: the pools auto, apps, people, devices, and the mode default.
  • Reserved: and, or, not, if, present, none, mode, and ids starting with state_ or slot_ (they would collide with entity ids in Home Assistant).
  • Sigils: @name a preset, #name a tag.

items.title: Conditions
items.text:
One expression language says "when" everywhere: in candidates ("mic if call") and in composed states (when = "...").

expr     := or
or       := and ("or" and)*
and      := not ("and" not)*
not      := "not" not | atom
atom     := ID | "present" | "present(" ID ")" | "(" expr ")"
  • ID: a state or mode; default is on while no other mode is.
  • present: the candidate's own channel or pool is present; only in candidates (a state takes channels with its source channels). present(spotify): that channel or pool is.
  • Errors point at the place: slots.7[0]: "voip if cal": unknown state cal (did you mean call?), with a caret in the GUI and check-config.

Conditions depend only on inputs, states and presence, never on what other slots show (the presence of a pool is counted before slots are assigned). That makes the resolver deterministic and Simulate truthful.

items.title: An example
items.text:
The author's configuration (example.toml; about 110 lines in the old format):

[channel.out]
type = "output"
color = "cyan"
choices = [ ... ]   # Phones, Speaker, Buds

[channel.browser]
type = "apps"
match = ["@browsers"]
label = "Browser"
color = "blue"
meter = true

[channel.game]
type = "apps"
match = ["@games"]
label = "Game"

[channel.voip]
type = "apps"
match = ["@voip"]
label = "VoIP"
color = "yellow"
lit_when_idle = true
in_pool = false             # notification sounds of Discord don't take an auto slot

[channel.mic]
type = "input"
device = "alsa_input.pci-0000_11_00.4.analog-stereo"
label = "Mic"
color = "red"
encoder = "balance"

[pool.auto]
color = "white"

[pool.people]               # they take auto slots from the right (next to VoIP), applications from the left
color = "yellow"

[state.gaming]
mode = true
label = "Gaming"
processes = ["@steam-games"]
apps = ["@games"]

[state.call]
voice_chat = true
recording = ["discord", "vesktop"]
delay_on = 0               # voice_chat and recording have no blips to swallow
delay_off = 5               # VoIP and Mic stay through a reconnect, not much longer

[slots]
1 = "out"                       # always the speaker/phones/buds
2 = "browser"
3 = ["game if gaming", "auto"]  # the game next to the browser
4 = [{ show = "auto", rec = "recording" }]
7 = ["voip if call", "auto"]
8 = ["mic if call", "auto"]

What it shows, as xtouch-daemon simulate docs/development/design/slots/example.toml --table prints it (a test keeps this table in line with the file): one row per combination of the states and presence the stacks ask about that changes something.

when             1    2        3     4-6   7     8
default          out  browser  auto  auto  auto  auto
call             out  browser  auto  auto  voip  mic
gaming           out  browser  game  auto  auto  auto
gaming and call  out  browser  game  auto  voip  mic
  • People share the auto slots: they sit from the right, next to VoIP, in their order; applications fill from the left. They meet only when the slots run out.
  • With Mumble, joining a channel turns call on at once (delay_on = 0): VoIP, Mic and the person show up together. Leaving shows at once on the person's strip; VoIP and Mic stay 5 s, through a reconnect.
  • Slot 4 sets an option of its strip, rec (here its default: the Rec LED shows recording).

items.title: A new configuration
items.text:
init-config writes the smallest configuration that works, and the rest as comments that teach it:

[channel.out]
type = "output"             # the default output

[channel.mic]
type = "input"              # the default input

[slots]
7 = "mic"
8 = "out"                   # the main output on the right, as in a DAW; slots 1 to 6 are auto

# [state.call]               # in a call, for slots like 6 = ["voip if call", "auto"]
# voice_chat = true          # Mumble with the plugin; for Discord: recording = ["discord"]
# delay_off = 5
#
# [state.gaming]             # a mode: while a game from Steam runs
# mode = true
# processes = ["@steam-games"]

items.title: Channels and pools
items.text: Part of Design: channels, states and slots.

items.title: Channels: what a strip controls
items.text:
A channel is the old strip without its place: type and the options of that type. The table key is its id.

[channel.out]
type = "output"
color = "cyan"

[[channel.out.choices]]
label = "Phones"
device = "alsa_output.pci-0000_11_00.4.analog-stereo"
card = "alsa_card.pci-0000_11_00.4"
profile = "output:analog-stereo+input:analog-stereo"

[[channel.out.choices]]
label = "Buds"
device = "bluez_output.*"

[channel.spotify]
type = "apps"
match = ["spotify"]
tags = ["media"]

[channel.alice]
type = "person"
person = ["Alice", "alice-phone"]
label = "Mum"
  • Types: output, input (choices), apps, homeassistant, and person (one person of the voice chat, with talking_color, max_volume, meter). Two person channels with a name in common are an error. A deliberately empty slot is the candidate "-".
  • tags: free-form names for grouping channels, used by pools (#media) and the channels source of states. They are no conditions; name them after what the channels are (media, games), not after states.
  • Presence: whether the channel has something to control: its device is there, an application of the group has a stream, the person is in the voice chat; always for homeassistant. absent_after (default 3 s) delays "absent", so a reconnecting Bluetooth device does not flap; it is present again at once.
  • in_pool (default true, apps and person channels): whether the channel joins the pools while it is present and no slot shows it: an apps channel apps and auto (as a whole: its label, volume and entities, as in DAW banking), a person channel people and auto (as itself).
  • Its entities are named by its id (select.xtouch_out_output), the same wherever and whenever it shows, and stay available while it is not shown. One owner per stream: the channel, wherever it is.

items.title: Pools: one of several
items.text:
A pool gives each slot that shows it one member that no other slot shows.

Pool Members Options apps The applications that play and have no channel, and the present apps channels with in_pool that have no slot. In the order they started playing; a member stays one hold seconds after it stopped. [pool.apps]: from ("left"), exclude (never these), hold (5 s), the look of the strips of applications. people The people in the voice chat without a person channel, and the present person channels with in_pool that have no slot. In order, then as first seen. See Where the people sit. [pool.people]: from ("right"), order, the look of the strips of people (color, talking_color, meter, meter_point, max_volume). auto Both: people and applications share its slots, the people first, each from its side. [pool.auto]: the look of the strips of applications on its slots. devices The outputs and inputs that no output or input channel has (a USB headset). auto doesn't take them. [pool.devices]: from, exclude (node names or descriptions, wildcards), hold, the look. [pool.<id>] channels = [...] The present channels of the list (ids, "#tag") that have no candidate of their own that shows, in the list's order. channels, from. Its members bring their own look.
  • Presence of a pool, for if present, counts its members before slots are assigned: apps while an application it may take plays; people while someone who would be one of them is in the voice chat (also a person channel with a slot of its own); auto while either is; devices while a device without a channel is there; a pool of channels while one of them is present.
  • from is "left" (slot 1 first) or "right" (slot 8 first). Inside auto the people fill from [pool.people] from, the applications from [pool.apps] from. The defaults are opposite sides, so people and applications meet only when the slots run out.
  • Members keep their slot in apps and auto, so applications don't hop around. People sit in their order instead, and a pool of channels fills by its order (the first present channel gets the first slot): Buds coming back takes its place, the others move on.
  • Members are typed: an application, a channel or a person, never told apart by their names (someone called browser is no channel). People are told apart by the voice chat's id of the participant; order and the learned order go by name.
  • Select does what it does on the member (makes a device the default, launches).
  • Pick (the pick encoder of a slot of apps or auto): turning picks the slot's member among the applications without a slot (2/5; people are never picked); a push pins it, and it stays on the slot after it stopped playing, until the next push. A pin beats the pool's order, and people don't take a pinned slot. The resolver keeps the pins: the encoder only asks for one.
  • Channels of a pool without a slot don't wait: only applications and people do; such channels are not shown.

items.title: In the daemon
items.text: Part of Design: channels, states and slots. The modules are in Architecture.

items.title: The runtime
items.text:
Slots replace the strips and layouts of the old format in the daemon natively (no translation into strips): parts that live as long as the daemon, the configuration or a member, and a binder that changes only the slots whose result changed.

Part Lives as long as What Desk (runtime/desk.py) the daemon The 8 strips of the device: touches, held buttons and touchless faders (held_slots()), the events to the presenter bound to each slot or to a claim, the meters of what is bound, banners and flashes. SlotEngine (runtime/slots.py) the daemon The StateEngine, presence, the members of the pools, the resolver with dwell, pins and the order of the people; keeps overrides, the mode picked and the people across restarts; wakes at the deadlines of the delays (no polling). A reload carries its state over by state, channel and member id. SlotMixer (runtime/binder.py) the configuration A controller with its own VirtualStrip per channel, per application of auto and per person without a channel while they are members (made when it becomes one, closed when its hold or absent_after ends; it moves between slots unchanged). Binds only the slots whose result changed; a controller gets its look and the options of its place when it is bound, its identity is its channel or member. Controls (runtime/controls.py) the configuration The [controls] of each slot with their entities, bound to the Desk's slot, not to what it shows. SlotEntities (runtime/homeassistant.py) the configuration The entities of the states, overrides, the mode and the slots.
  • Times come from the loop's clock (loop.time()).
  • The Desk routes by slot and control (fader, encoder, each button) to an owner: the bound presenter or a claim. It is sticky: a release goes to whoever got the press, even if a bind() came in between. A touched fader goes over instead: on bind() the presenter that had it gets on_touch(False), the new one on_touch(True), its moves and its release, so each sees a touch and its release. A live preview uses the same Desk, so touches and held buttons carry over its start and end.

items.title: Home Assistant
items.text: Entity What The entities of a channel (number.xtouch_<id>_fader, select.xtouch_<id>_output, ...) Named by the channel id, registered once per configuration: they stay available (and keep their state) while the channel is not shown or moves; the buttons of a homeassistant channel send events only while it is shown. The entities of the controls of a slot (number.xtouch_slot_<n>_fader, event.xtouch_slot_<n>_buttons, ..., or <id> instead of slot_<n>) Registered once per configuration, whatever the slot shows. binary_sensor.xtouch_<id>_shown Whether the channel is on a slot. sensor.xtouch_slot_<n> What slot n shows: a channel id, app:<application>, person:<name>, or none. Attributes label, kind (channel, app, person, none), via (the candidate), reason. binary_sensor.xtouch_state_<id> The state. Attributes since, source (which source turned it on), override. select.xtouch_state_<id> The override: auto, on, off. switch.xtouch_state_<id>_input Only with homeassistant = true: what Home Assistant feeds into the state. select.xtouch_mode The mode override: auto and every mode.

items.title: Commands
items.text:
• check-config prints the channels, the outcome table and its notes (see Slots).
  • list-apps says per application which channel, pool or slot has it.
  • why <slot or channel> tells what a slot shows and why not the candidates above it, or where a channel is and why not elsewhere (browser: on slot 2; not slot 8 (on slot 2 (tie, to the left))); why people who sits where and who waits.
  • simulate and observe: the slots of a file in any situation, and a recording of the real system to replay (simulate --replay).

items.title: The GUI
items.text:
• Slots: each slot is a card with its stack, a row per candidate with its condition as text chips (call or gaming, always) and a tiny LCD in the color of its strip, ▶ on the one shown. Drag and drop or Ctrl+Up/Down reorder. The inspector edits the candidate (condition, the options for this place), says where else its channel is used and what a pool hands out and from where; below it the slot's controls. The why line is the resolver's trace.
  • Simulate: what-if inputs (every state, the presence the stacks ask about, how many people are in the call and applications play); the drawing shows what the resolver would, in the GUI or on the device where "Preview" says, see Previews. Esc ends it.
  • The state bar is live: each state with its value and since when; its menu sets the override, and an overridden state is hatched, with ⟲ back to auto.
  • Channels: channels and pools (the built-in ones below, each with the look of its strips), with type, label, tags and where they are used; Add, Duplicate, Remove.
  • States: modes first, then the other states: sources or when, delays, persist, the live value since when and from which source, the override, and which stacks use it.
  • Problems link to a slot, candidate, channel, pool or state. The GUI keeps the form a stack has in the file (string, compact list or tables) and its comments.

items.title: Where the people sit
items.text: Part of Design: channels, states and slots. Status: built (2026-11-17), the third round of the design. Its rules are in Pools and the resolver.

items.title: Why
items.text:
At first the people of the voice chat had no candidate of their own: the resolver put them on the slots of auto from the right, while applications filled them from the left. That fits one layout (the voice chat's strips on the right), and the file could say nothing else: not the voice chat on the left, not people in the middle, not people only in a call, not "a call replaces the applications". The GUI didn't show that auto takes people at all.

So there are three built-in pools, each a candidate like any channel: apps (the applications), people (the people) and auto (both, sharing its slots, the people first). A pool hands a slot it has no member for to the pool or - right below it, so ["people", "apps"] is a person, else an application.

items.title: Not a block
items.text: People inside auto (and in people) are no block: they take the slots where nothing is above them first, then the others, each group from their side. In the live test's file with call overridden off the order was 6, 5, 4, then 8, 7, 3, 2. This stays, for a reason: people keep no slot (they sit in their order, recomputed every step), so a slot that a candidate above can take back (voip if call) would move every one of them when it does. Applications keep the slot they had, so for them the side alone decides (as before: slot 2 before slot 3, whatever is above them).

items.title: Use cases
items.text: A, B, ... are people in their order; "call" is the state call (Mumble: voice_chat = true). The tables come from the resolver (without a previous result).

On 2 and 3 applications come before people: in a crowded call a playing application still gets a fader. A dark slot shows the last pool of its chain (people on 2 and 3).

items.text:

items.title: Not chosen
items.text:
• People only as a pool, pools never fall through: slots meant for people are dark outside a call (the live test rejected that).
  • auto alone with options in [people] (from, slots, when, alone): a second language next to the stacks.
  • A preference per auto place (people = "first"): the same as stacks, hidden in an option.
  • A list of slots for people ([people] slots = [6, 5, 4]): a second place to edit when a slot moves.
  • A real block, or "first candidate first" for applications too: see Not a block.
  • +2 or paging when more people than slots: they wait; the why line and the live view say who.

items.title: Pools of your own
items.text: Part of Design: channels, states and slots. Status: built (2026-11-19). Without kind, a [pool.<id>] lists channels (Pools); the pools of applications, people and devices are built in. This page adds pools of applications and of people that the user defines.

items.title: Why
items.text:
The built-in apps pool hands out every application that plays and has no slot, in the order they started. That is one pool for everything. Wishes it can't express:

  • "The music players on slot 5, whatever else plays": apps would put a browser tab there as well.
  • "My friends first, on the left": the pool people has one order, one side and one look for everybody.
  • Two groups of applications on different sides of the device, each in its own color.

A channel can't do it either: an apps channel is one strip over all its streams, and one fader moves them together. What is missing is a pool that selects the applications (or people) that qualify, and still gives each its own strip.

items.title: The format
items.text:
[pool.<id>] gets an optional kind. Without it, the section is a pool of channels, as today, so no file changes.

[pool.music]
kind = "apps"
match = ["@music"]            # presets and parts of names, as in an `apps` channel
exclude = ["spotify-ads"]     # optional: never these, though they match
from = "left"                 # the side it fills its slots from (default)
hold = 5                      # seconds a slot keeps an application after it stopped (default)
color = "green"               # the look of its strips, as in [pool.apps]

[pool.friends]
kind = "people"
people = ["Alice", "Bob"]     # names in the voice chat; this order is their order
from = "right"                # default: left for apps, right for people, as the built-in pools
color = "yellow"
talking_color = "green"

[slots]
5 = ["music", "apps"]         # a music player if one plays, else the next other application
6 = ["friends", "people"]     # Alice and Bob first, then anyone else in the call

Two kinds, no mixed pool. A pool of applications and a pool of people share a slot by being two candidates of its stack (["friends", "music", "auto"]), as the built-in ones do.

Option kind = "apps" kind = "people" match Required. Parts of application names or binaries, presets allowed. Not allowed. exclude Optional, as in [pool.apps]. Not allowed. people Not allowed. Required. Names as in person of a channel (case-insensitive, whole names). from Default left. Default right. hold Seconds, default 5. Not allowed: people stay absent_after seconds, like the built-in pool. look (color, meter, meter_point, rec, solo, lit_when_idle) The look options of [pool.apps]. The look options of [pool.people] (talking_color too). encoder, min_volume, max_volume As in [pool.apps], but no pick; default media. Not allowed: the strips of people have none.

Errors use the existing words: a missing match is pool.music: kind apps needs match; an option of the other kind names where it belongs (people: an option of kind people). A kind other than the two lists them.

items.title: What it takes
items.text:
Every member belongs to one source, and the first source that qualifies takes it. The order is fixed, from the most specific to the most general:

  1. Channels. An application of an apps channel that has a slot, and a person of a person channel, are the channel's, as today.
  2. Pools of your own, in the order of the file: pools of people, then pools of applications. A member that two of them could take goes to the one that comes first in the file.
  3. The built-in pools. apps and auto take the applications that nothing above took, people and auto the people.

So music takes a music player out of apps and auto, as an apps channel with a slot already does. A pool of your own takes its members only while a slot names it (in any stack, shown or not), like a channel with a slot. A pool that no slot names takes nothing, so a forgotten [pool.music] can't make the players disappear from the device; check-config says "pool music is on no slot".

auto stays what it is: the people and the applications that no channel and no pool of your own took.

items.title: How a slot is filled
items.text:
The resolver already hands members out in rounds, by kind (slots/resolver.py, _contest): per kind the slots that take it, each kind from its side, and a slot that two kinds could fill goes to the one higher in its stack. This page keeps those rules and changes what a "kind" is: today it is one of people, apps, devices, in future it is a source, and every pool of your own is one.

  • Chain and hand-down are unchanged: a pool with no member for a slot hands it to the candidate below it (a pool or -). A pool of your own is a pool in a chain like the others, and may be above or below any of them. The rule that channels end a chain stays.
  • Contest. A slot named by several sources goes to the source higher in its stack; a tie goes to the order of What it takes (your pools before the built-in ones). The loser gives the slot up and hands out again, until nothing changes. It ends for the same reason as today: a source only loses slots.
  • Fill order. Each source from its side. The people of a pool of people first take the slots where it is the first candidate (Not a block); a pool of applications keeps the slot each had.
  • Pins and pick. A pool of applications has no pick encoder (encoder = "pick" is an error): its default is media. Pins of the built-in pools work unchanged.
  • Waiting. Members that got no slot wait per source: Result.waiting keys are pool names, so why and the GUI say "Alice waits" for friends and "Spotify waits" for music.
  • Presence. present of a pool of your own is true while it has a member (an application plays, a listed person is in the voice chat), counted before slots are assigned, like the built-in pools.

items.title: Hold, absence and reload
items.text: hold and absent_after become per source: PoolMembers (slots/inputs.py) keeps one Lingering list per pool of your own, not one for apps. A reload carries them over by pool id (carry); a pool that is gone drops its list.

items.title: In the daemon
items.text: Where Change slots/model.py PoolConfig becomes a union on kind: channels (no kind), apps, people. Scene knows the pools of your own, their order, their members' rules (match, people) and their look. The names apps, people, auto, devices stay reserved. slots/inputs.py Membership by the order above; PoolMembers per pool; pool_present for the new kinds. slots/resolver.py KINDS, ORDER, kind_of: from three constants to the sources of the scene. Shown.pool is the pool of your own; Result.waiting keys likewise. slots/outcomes.py, why.py, simulation.py The table of check-config and Simulate count presence of the new pools; the notes say "pool X is on no slot" and "pool X can never show" (like a channel below a pool). Simulate gets counts for the members of each pool of your own, as for apps and people. runtime/slots.py, strips/ A strip for a member of a pool of your own is built like one of apps or people, with the look of its pool. live/messages.py, mqtt.py SlotView.pool carries the pool id; the HA sensor sensor.<ns>_slot_<n> shows app:<name> / person:<name> as before, with the pool in its attributes. GUI The Channels page gets "Pool of applications" and "Pool of people" in its Add menu and a form per kind (match, exclude or people, the side, the look). The slot card's chip names the pool and the member (music · Spotify). Docs configuration/slots.md (pools), channels/applications.md and people.md, concepts.md, the example in config.example.toml stays small.

items.title: Use cases
items.text: Applications are listed in the order they started; A, B are people in the order of people.

items.title: U1: music apart from the rest
items.text:
[pool.music] kind = "apps", match = ["@music"], 5 = ["music", "apps"], 6 = "apps".

Plays Slot 5 Slot 6 Firefox Firefox dark Spotify Spotify dark Firefox, Spotify Spotify Firefox Spotify stops, hold passes (Firefox plays on) dark Firefox

With only Firefox playing, music has no member and hands slot 5 down to apps, which fills from the left. When Spotify comes, music takes slot 5 back and Firefox moves to slot 6, the one slot left for apps. Once Spotify is gone, Firefox keeps slot 6 (applications keep their slot) and slot 5 goes dark: apps has no other member.

items.title: U2: friends first
items.text: [pool.friends] kind = "people", people = ["Alice", "Bob"], 6 = ["friends", "people"], 7 = ["people", "apps"]. In a call with Bob, Carol and Alice: slot 6 Alice (the first of the pool's own order), slot 7 Carol, Bob waits for friends' second slot, which does not exist. Bob is not handed to people either: a member of a pool of your own stays in it, so why says "Bob waits".

items.title: U3: a pool above auto
items.text: 3 = ["music", "auto"]: the players first, else the next application or person, as ["apps", "people"] would. The pool of your own wins a contest over auto on the same slot because it is higher in the stack.

items.title: Decisions to confirm
items.text:
1. Members are kept in their pool (U2): a person of friends who finds no slot waits, and does not fall into people. This keeps "who sits where" predictable and mirrors a channel with a slot. The alternative (fall through to the built-in pool when the slot's chain has one) gives Bob a slot, but then friends is no longer "the friends' strips".
  2. A pool of your own takes its members only while a slot names it. The alternative, always taking them, hides applications silently.
  3. kind = "devices" is not offered. The built-in devices pool has exclude already; a pool of devices of your own has no use case yet.
  4. No order in a pool of people. The list of names is the order. Members of the built-in people pool that are not listed sit after, as today.

items.title: Slots
items.text:
Part of Design: channels, states and slots.

The device has 8 slots, one per strip, numbered 1 to 8 from the left. Each has a stack of candidates, top first.

[slots]
1 = "out"                   # a single candidate: the same as ["out"]
2 = "browser"
3 = ["game if gaming", "auto"]
4 = [{ show = "auto", encoder = "pick" }]
7 = ["voip if call", "auto"]
8 = ["mic if call", "auto"]
  • A candidate is "<channel or pool>", optionally with " if <expression>", or "-": deliberately nothing (the slot is dark).
  • A slot without an entry is "auto". A stack whose candidates all don't hold, or lose, ends in an implicit "auto"; "-" at the end makes it dark instead.
  • Two words keep the rules apart: a candidate holds while its condition is true; a slot shows the candidate it gets in the end. A candidate without a condition always holds: an absent channel is shown dark and keeps its place, an empty pool hands down or is dark. "spotify if present" holds only while there is something.
  • Options for this place, in the table form { show = "...", when = "...", ... }:
  • on a channel, its look here: label, color, lit_when_idle, rec, solo, meter, meter_point; on a pool the same without label (its strips show the names of their members);
  • on apps and auto also what acts on an application without a channel: encoder (pick, media, volume, balance), min_volume, max_volume; on devices encoder (balance, volume), min_volume, max_volume, select; on people only color, meter and meter_point.
  • The built-in pools ([pool.apps], ...) take the same options as their places. A Home Assistant encoder or fader, launch and an id are controls of the slot, in [controls].
  • They apply to the members without a channel. A channel shown as a member looks and works as the channel; the place only fills in what it leaves open. What a control does whatever the slot shows is in [controls].

items.title: The resolver
items.text:
slots.resolver.resolve() decides what each slot shows from the inputs (states, presence, pool members, pins, held slots) and, for the members of apps, the previous result. Its trace is what why and the GUI tell.

  1. Fixed slots. A slot that is held (a finger, a button) or within its dwell time keeps what it shows; its channel or member is reserved, and the other slots are resolved around it.
  2. Channels by rank. Every other slot proposes its first candidate that holds. A channel that several slots propose goes to the one where it is highest in the stack (its rank), ties to the leftmost slot; the others go on to their next candidate that holds. Repeat until nothing changes. A pool takes its slot in this step (pools are not contested). It ends: a slot only goes down its stack.
  3. Pools. The members are handed out:
  4. Chain. The pool a slot shows after step 2, and the candidates below it that hold while they are pools, up to and with a -, form the slot's chain; a channel ends it. ["people if call", "- if call", "auto"] while call is on: people, -.
  5. Hand-down. A pool with no member for a slot leaves it to the next pool of the chain. A slot no pool fills shows the last pool of its chain, dark, or -.
  6. Pools of channels first, in the order of the file, each from its side. One below apps, people or auto in a chain is an error: those take the channels that no pool of channels gives a slot.
  7. Contest. Then the people over the slots whose chain has people or auto, in their order; the applications over those with apps or auto: pins first, then each on the slot it had, then in their order. A slot both fill goes to the one higher in its stack (inside auto, the people); the other gives it up and is handed out again, until nothing changes. It ends: each only loses slots. Members left over wait.
  8. Fill order. Each from its side; the people first take the slots where they are the first candidate, then the others (see Not a block).
  9. A pin reserves its slot if the chain there has apps or auto; a pin waits while a held slot shows its member, and a pin of a channel that has a slot of its own is dropped (one channel, one slot).

Conditions never look at the result, so the steps run once each, in this order: the same inputs give the same result.

items.title: Stability
items.text:
• Batching: changes are resolved together 0.1 s after the first one (runtime/slots.BATCH): a game starts several streams and a process at once, and the faders move once.
  • Dwell: a slot keeps what it shows for at least 1 s before it changes again (slots/simulation.DWELL).
  • Nothing changes under a finger: a held slot is fixed (step 1) until let go, with its claims. A fader in touchless_faders counts as touched while the user moves it and half a second after; the motor moving it doesn't count. The buttons of the chord don't hold slots.
  • Startup: the daemon waits for the first state of the sound server and the first process scan, evaluates the states without delay_on (the baseline), restores the overrides, and only then runs the startup sequence: the first picture is the right one.
  • Reload: the previous result carries over by channel id and member.

items.title: Telling what changed
items.text: A slot that shows something else flashes the new label on the top line and why on the bottom line (the when of the new candidate, or not <when> of the old one) for switching.banner seconds. A new mode shows its label across all LCDs instead. The motor fader moves to the new volume, as with banking in a DAW. The log has one line per change with the reasons.

items.title: Controls
items.text:
What a fader, encoder or button of a slot does whatever the slot shows: actions of the place, not of a channel.

[controls]
4 = { encoder = "homeassistant" }                        # number.xtouch_slot_4_encoder and push events
7 = { select = { launch = ["mumble", "mumble://..."] }, when = "not call" }
1 = { solo = "toggle:night", rec = "homeassistant" }
2 = { fader = "homeassistant", id = "desk_fader" }       # number.xtouch_desk_fader_fader
3 = [                                                    # the first whose when holds
    { encoder = "homeassistant", id = "strip_3", when = "gaming" },
    { select = { launch = ["obs"] } },
]
  • What can be claimed: fader, encoder (turn and push), select, rec and solo; not Mute, which stays with what the slot shows, and not the Solo buttons of the chord.
  • Actions: "homeassistant" (a number for the fader or encoder, events for the buttons, a select for their LED), { launch = [...], launch_when_running = ... }, and the actions of the chord: "cycle_modes", "mode:<id>", "toggle:<state>" (the LED shows the state). "toggle:<mode>" picks the mode, and the next press gives it back to the rules; its LED is on while it is the mode. A fader and an encoder only take "homeassistant".
  • One table or a list: the first entry whose when (states only, no present) holds acts. The entries of a slot may share an id; another slot can't have it.
  • A claim wins over what the slot shows and owns its LED or ring; the presenter bound there is told which controls are taken. With the fader taken, the encoder of what the slot shows sets the volume; with only the encoder taken, the fader stays the volume. A candidate can't set the LED (rec, solo) of a claimed button, also while the claim's when doesn't hold: one owner per LED in the file.
  • A channel's own fader/encoder = "homeassistant" (entities by channel id, moving with the channel) stays; a claim of the slot wins while it holds.
  • Controls don't touch the resolver: they hold no slot, and people and channels sit there as anywhere. A release goes to whoever got the press.
  • Entities: *.xtouch_slot_<n>_*, or *.xtouch_<id>_* with id: registered once per configuration, always there, following the slot rather than what it shows.

items.title: Pitfalls
items.text:
• Launch behind a condition. A channel's launch works only while a slot shows it. "voip if call" hides VoIP exactly when you'd press Select to start the voice chat: put the launch into [controls] with when = "not call".
  • Hidden indicators. A hidden channel's LEDs are not on the device: mic if call hides the Mic and its Rec LED, which lights while any application records (a meeting in a browser tab).
  • A voice chat without room. People in a call while no slot is free for them wait; the why line says so ("Bob waits").
  • Rank surprises. 1 = ["buds if present", "out"] and 3 = ["out if video", "auto"]: in video mode without buds, out goes to slot 3 (rank 1 there, 2 on slot 1), and slot 1 shows auto. Correct, but only the outcome table, Simulate or why make it visible.

check-config's notes (slots/outcomes.notes()) name a channel right below a pool without a condition (it never shows) and people with no slot to sit on.

items.title: States and modes
items.text:
Part of Design: channels, states and slots.

A state is a named condition that is on or off, evaluated all the time and visible everywhere: the GUI, the live view, Home Assistant.

[state.call]
voice_chat = true           # in a channel of the voice chat, also alone (from the bridge)
recording = ["discord", "vesktop"]   # or: one of these records (they open a capture stream only in a call)
delay_off = 5               # stays 5 s after: a reconnect, not much longer

[state.wireless]
devices = ["bluez_output.*"]

[state.focus]
when = "not call and not gaming"

[state.night]
homeassistant = true        # Home Assistant feeds it: switch.xtouch_state_night_input

items.title: Sources
items.text:
Source On while apps One of these applications has a playback stream (playing or paused). Names and presets as match. recording One of these applications has a capture stream. Not for Mumble, which keeps its capture open while connected, even alone; use voice_chat. voice_chat The voice chat reports that you are in a channel, also alone: joining one says you mean to talk (the mic shows before anyone comes, and the pool people covers who comes). processes A process of one of these names runs (polled every 2 s while any state uses it). devices A device (output or input) that matches is there. channels One of these channels is present: ids, or "#tag". homeassistant Its input switch in Home Assistant (switch.xtouch_state_<id>_input) is on. when The expression holds. Not with other sources: a state is either composed or has sources.
  • A state with several sources is on while any of them is. Without sources it is only what its override says.
  • Delays: delay_on (default 0) and delay_off (default 3 s; 10 s for modes) apply to the sources, not to the override. A composed state has none by default: its expression has the delays of what it names, so call and not call never overlap. Delays given to it apply to its expression.
  • References between states and modes must not form a loop; check-config names it.

items.title: Overrides
items.text:
Every state has an override: auto (the sources decide), on or off, set from Home Assistant (select.xtouch_state_<id>), the GUI or a button (the chord, [controls]). One rule for all states and modes:

  • on and off take effect at once, past the delays; back to auto, the sources decide at once too.
  • An override lasts until the sources change (an edge after their delays), then it is auto again. Example: gaming forced off while a game runs (to use the default mode for a moment); when the game exits, auto again, and the next game brings the mode. So an override set while a delay_on is pending ends when the delay does.
  • persist = true keeps it across edges, until it is set to auto by hand. States without sources have no edges, so their override is kept by itself.
  • Overrides are kept across restarts. The first evaluation after a start is the baseline, not an edge: a kept override survives it.
  • An active override shows: hatched in the GUI's state bar, override in Home Assistant's attributes, and in the banner on the LCDs when it is set and when the daemon starts.

items.title: Modes
items.text:
Modes are states with mode = true. Exactly one mode is on: the one with the highest priority whose sources are on (then the first in the file), else default. A mode has a label, the banner across the LCDs.

[state.gaming]
mode = true
label = "Gaming"
processes = ["@steam-games"]
apps = ["@games"]
  • The override is one: select.xtouch_mode with auto and every mode, xtouch-daemon mode gaming, mode --next/--previous, mode auto. --next and the chord cycle through default and the modes in the order of the file (not through auto).
  • A picked mode lasts until the rules want another mode than before: edges that don't change what the rules want (a mode of lower priority starts) and edges of modes with persist don't end it.

items.title: The chord
items.text: [switching] chord = { strips = [1, 8], action = "cycle_modes" } (the default): the Solo buttons of those strips held together. action = "mode:<id>" picks a mode, "toggle:<state>" toggles the override of a state (auto, the opposite of its value now, auto). The same actions are those of buttons in [controls]; the Solo buttons of the chord can't be claimed there and don't hold slots.

items.title: History: strips that move
items.text: Status: built on the old format, then replaced by channels, states and slots before 0.1.0. Its other half, one strip switching between outputs, stays: Design: output choices.

items.title: Collapsing strips
items.text:
collapse = true on a strip: while it had nothing to control (no device, no stream, no participant) for behavior.collapse_hold seconds, it gave up its fader and the strips after it moved left. A file could list up to 32 strips; the first 8 present ones got the faders, the rest waited. Placement waited while a finger was on the device, and each change was logged ("Strips: Buds appears at 2, Browser moves to 3, Spotify waits").

It went because the fader under the finger changed with things far away from it, which hurts muscle memory. Now a channel keeps its slot ("buds if present" above auto), and a pool of channels fills by its order for those who want moving strips.

items.title: inherit from any layout and strip
items.text: type = "inherit" with layout and strip (a position or an id) took another layout's strip, with chains resolved and loops an error. State was not shared across layouts: a layout switch built new controllers. It went with the layouts; a channel now is the same one wherever it shows.

items.title: History: layouts
items.text:
Status: replaced by channels, states and slots before 0.1.0. What stays of it: the research below, and the voice chat, which was designed with it.

The idea: several layouts, each a set of up to 8 strips ([[layout]] with [[layout.strip]]; the top-level [[strip]] list was the layout default). One was active; rules (apps, processes, priority) picked it, edge-triggered with a hold, and Home Assistant (select.<ns>_layout), the command line (xtouch-daemon layout), the GUI (a tab per layout) and the Solo chord switched by hand. A switch was a reload with another set of strips on the same surface, with a banner across the LCDs. inherit strips took the strip of another layout at their place; voip strips without person formed a group that paged through the participants with Select.

What carried over: edge-triggered rules and a manual choice that lasts until they change (now the overrides of modes), the banner, the chord, the remembered choice, voice_chat and the people.

What didn't work: a strip that matters in two situations needed two layouts that can't both be active; inherit referred to positions, so moving a strip changed what it meant. See why.

items.title: What others do
items.text:
Product Unit How it switches Notes Elgato Stream Deck profile, with pages and folders "Smart Profiles": the application in focus picks its profile, matched by executable; leaving it restores the previous profile. A key action switches by hand. (Elgato) Automatic switching is paused while the editor is open. A manual switch by a plugin can disable the automatic one (bug report), a known pain point. Loupedeck / Logitech profile per application, with workspaces and pages "Dynamic mode" (on by default) follows the active application; off, the chosen profile stays. A button switches workspaces. (Loupedeck CT, user guide) Open-source Linux ports match by process name and window title, falling back to a default profile (loupedeckapp). GoXLR Utility (Linux) device and microphone profiles UI, and goxlr-client profiles device load <name> for scripts and hotkeys (wiki) The profile is a whole mixer state; a "load colours only" variant exists. Mackie Control DAWs (Logic, Cubase) banks of 8 channels Bank Left/Right moves by 8 (by the size of the surface group), Channel Left/Right by 1; the last bank is filled up to 8 rather than left half empty (Logic) The model for "more participants than strips". deej one configuration none; the file is reloaded on change (From the project's README, not re-checked.) Voicemeeter settings files, macro buttons macro buttons and the Remote API load a settings file (From memory, not re-checked.) TouchOSC pages (tabs) of one layout a tab bar on the surface, or OSC/MIDI messages (From memory, not re-checked.)

Lessons taken:

  1. One active layout, switched as a whole. Every product swaps the complete set of controls; nobody blends two.
  2. Automatic and manual switching coexist, and the rules for that must be simple. Stream Deck and Loupedeck make the automatic one win whenever the focus changes; a manual choice lasts until the next change. That was the model here too: rules are edge-triggered.
  3. Focus is a desktop concept. On Wayland there is no portable way to ask which window has the focus (KWin scripts, GNOME extensions, the Sway/Hyprland IPC all differ). The daemon knows something better for a mixer: which applications play (PipeWire streams), and which processes run (/proc). Focus can come later as a provider of the same rule engine.
  4. A command line to switch (GoXLR) makes every other integration (hotkeys, scripts, desktop launchers) free.
  5. Banks for variable lists (Mackie): a group of strips shows a page of a longer list, and buttons page through it.

items.title: History: refactoring, November 2026
items.text: Status: done (2026-11-18). A pass over the code for structure, without changing what anything does. The steps were ranked by value against risk; each was one commit, checked with ruff, pyright and the tests that cover it.

items.title: Survey
items.text:
• 26 000 lines in src/. The layers hold: no Qt in gui/domain, nothing outside gui/ imports the GUI, pyright passes on src/.
  • The large modules: gui/qt/window/main_window.py (1100 lines), gui/qt/pages/slots.py (935), slots/model.py (785), gui/qt/preview/strip_view.py (700), runtime/daemon.py (640).
  • MainWindow builds the rail, the settings navigation, the menus, the header and the footer, filters the keys and the wheel of the whole application, decides which page shows a problem, and runs the service, the file, the zoom and "Try without a device".
  • SlotsPanel holds the widgets of a card (StackList, CandidateRow, the chips of a rule) next to the page, and decides in the widget what belongs to the domain: where a candidate stands against the one shown, which strip type the place of a candidate has, and what a pool hands out on a slot.
  • Dead code: demos.AUDIO_TYPES and Preview.drop_target are used nowhere.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Dead code. Remove demos.AUDIO_TYPES and Preview.drop_target.
  2. Decisions of the page Slots into the domain. slot_stacks gets row_state() (a candidate against the one shown), place_strip() (the strip type of a place) and member_summary() (what a pool hands out on a slot and who waits). The page calls them; they can be tested without Qt.
  3. The cards of the page Slots in a module of their own. gui/qt/pages/slot_cards.py gets StackList, CandidateRow, the chips and the rule of a candidate, and filling a card. pages/slots.py keeps the page: the bars, the inspector, Simulate and the edits.
  4. Where a problem is shown, in the domain. gui/domain/problems.py has place_of(problem): the page (and the channel, state or slot on it) that shows a problem. MainWindow.go_to() only goes there.
  5. The filter of the keys and the wheel. gui/qt/window/input_filter.py: the application-wide filter that keeps Undo and Redo from the text fields and the wheel from fields that would change their value. MainWindow installs it and removes it when it closes.
  6. The rail and the settings in a module of their own. gui/qt/window/rail.py: Rail (the pages, their names shown or not) and SettingsPages (the navigation and the stack of the settings). MainWindow keeps rail_buttons and nav_buttons for the tests and show_page().
  7. The geometry of a Session. The conversion between the pixels of the screen and those of the window is one function, scaled(), instead of written out twice.
  8. The files of the slots. runtime/slots.py keeps the SlotEngine; reading and writing slots.json and people.json go to runtime/slot_files.py.

After these, the architecture names the new modules.

items.title: Left as they are
items.text:
• runtime/daemon.py. One lifecycle: reload, preview and the run loop share the configuration that runs and the mixer. Splitting the preview off would hand the same state around, not make it simpler.
  • gui/qt/preview/strip_view.py. Long, but one thing: painting a strip and the hand on it. Its paint methods share the state of the strip and the cached pictures.
  • slots/model.py. The pydantic models of the configuration with their validators; the length is their docstrings, which the GUI shows as help.
  • strips/. The controller hierarchy is the extension point of the channel types; it is not duplicated.
  • The live protocol, the configuration format, the MQTT entities and the CLI. Untouched, as for any refactoring.
  • Tests that fail already. They are the owner's to fix; a test only gets a moved import.

items.title: History: channels, states and slots
items.text: How the design of channels, states and slots came to be, from the old format of strips and layouts to 0.1.0. The design itself has only what holds now.

items.title: How it was built
items.text:
Three reviews of the prose found three rounds of holes, each in the parts that only existed as prose, so the resolver and the state engine became code first (xtouch_daemon.slots, pure, driven by xtouch-daemon simulate), then a prototype on the device, then the daemon natively. Each step kept the daemon working and the tests green:

  1. The format, read and checked ([controls] ran from step 5 on).
  2. The Desk out of the old Mixer, for both formats: touches and held buttons survive a new mixer.
  3. Controllers get their look, identity and entity ids from outside.
  4. The SlotEngine with pins, overrides and persistence, carried over a reload; typed members.
  5. The slots natively: a controller per channel and member, [controls], the binder on the Desk; entities per channel and per slot's controls.
  6. Home Assistant: states, overrides, the mode (replacing the layout select), the slots; the chord's new form.
  7. The live view: the snapshot of slots and states, the requests SetMode and SetOverride.
  8. check-config, init-config, the docs.
  9. The old format and its runtime went (decided 2026-11-17, before step 10, so the GUI could not edit configurations in between): Mixer, placement.py, layouts.py, AutoAssigner, VoipSeats, collapse, inherit, select.<ns>_layout, the layout parts of the live view. parse_config refuses [[strip]] and [[layout]]; xtouch-daemon layout fails with a pointer to mode.
  10. The GUI edits the new format: the document with option paths, the rail, Channels, States, the slot cards, why, Simulate (and a grid of the distinct outcomes, removed later).

The people were decided again in a third round (Where the people sit), which replaced [people] with [pool.people], in_auto with in_pool, and made apps, people and auto built-in pools.

items.title: What building it showed
items.text:
• An override set while a delay is pending ends with it. call forced off while a join tone's delay_on runs: 2 s later the sources turn on (an edge), the override ends, and the call comes anyway. That is the rule ("until the sources change"); whether it is what people expect needs trying on the device.
  • The grid explains rank surprises. A test configuration with 1 = ["buds if present", "out"] and 3 = ["out if video", "auto"]: in video mode without buds, out goes to slot 3 (rank 1 there, 2 on slot 1), and slot 1 shows auto. Correct, but only the grid (or check-config's list of shared channels) makes it visible.
  • present on "-" meant nothing: now an error.
  • Channels of a pool without a slot don't wait: only applications and people do; such channels are just not shown.
  • A multi-line inline table is no TOML 1.0: the examples of choices use [[channel.out.choices]].
