5 = ["people", "apps"]
6 = ["people", "apps"]
7 = ["voip if call", "apps"]
8 = ["mic if call", "apps"]

Where to go from here: Channels, states and slots for what else a slot can do (pools, modes, controls), Home Assistant, Troubleshooting.

items.title: Without a device
items.text: A virtual X-Touch Extender stands in for the device, e.g. to follow the Setup tour before the device arrives, to try a configuration, or while the device is away. It speaks the bytes of the real one, so the daemon does the same with it, down to faders that wait for a touch; Hardware lists what it does like the device and what is assumed.

items.title: In the GUI
items.text:
xtouch-daemon gui

"Try without a device" above the drawing starts a daemon with the virtual device inside the window: the drawing is the device, and the mouse on it is a hand on it (Play: press a fader to touch it, drag to move it, click a button; see GUI). The daemon ends with the window. Nothing else to set up.

items.title: In terminals
items.text:
xtouch-daemon virtual-device                # the device, headless, until Ctrl+C
xtouch-daemon test --virtual-device         # the self-test of the device, see First steps
xtouch-daemon run --virtual-device          # or [device] virtual = true: the daemon drives it
xtouch-daemon gui                           # shows what the daemon shows

The pill on the bar of the window Device in the GUI says "virtual device not running · Open it" while the daemon waits for the device: a click opens it in the window, and the mouse on the drawing is a hand on the device (see GUI). One daemon at a time can use the virtual device.

A daemon that runs but finds no device switches to the virtual one without a restart: "Use the virtual device" above the drawing sets [device] virtual = true, saves and opens it, and Play on a daemon that waits for the virtual device opens it too. Setting virtual back to false and saving switches to the real device again.

items.title: GUI
items.text:
xtouch-daemon gui edits the configuration file in a window and applies it to the running daemon. It starts with xtouch-daemon-gui (the Arch Linux package) or xtouch-daemon gui, -c FILE for another file; see Install.

It edits channels, states and slots. New here? The Setup tour builds a configuration with it, page by page; this page is the reference.

items.title: The window
items.text:
The window Configuration has a rail of four pages on its left, icons only (» at its foot shows their names, « hides them again; the GUI remembers it):

  • Slots: what each slot shows when, see The slots.
  • Channels: two groups: the channels (each takes one strip), then the pools (each supplies a member to every slot that names it): the built-in [pool.apps], [pool.people], [pool.auto] and [pool.devices]. The box Shows of a candidate on the page Slots has the same two groups. Add (by type, or a pool of channels of your own), Duplicate and Remove; the id of a channel or pool can be renamed (the slots, conditions, pools and controls that name it follow). Each says where it is used (slot 2, pool games, state call).
  • States: the modes first, then the other states. The form asks in order: State or Mode (a mode has a label and a priority), and On while: Sources or Condition, never both. Sources lists only the ones the state has, each with ✕ to remove it; Add source offers the others ("An application plays", "You are in the voice chat", ...), and the state is on while any of them is. Condition takes a condition of other states and modes, in the field of the page Slots. Switching between them asks before it removes what the other had. Delays and overrides (delay_on, delay_off, persist) are folded away until a state has one. Above the form: what the daemon says about it right now (since when, from which source), its override (a mode: picked by hand), and which stacks and controls use it.
  • Settings: [behavior], [aliases], [mqtt] (as "Home Assistant"), [switching] (as "Modes and chord"), [voip] (as "Voice chat") and [device] (as "Extender": the sound card of the extender, touch sensors, start-up). "Voice chat" also tells whether Mumble is connected, lists the steps of its setup, and installs the Mumble plugin with "Install Mumble plugin".

Slots, Channels and States have a list or the slots on the left and what is picked on the right. The handle between them (the short upright bar) gives either side more room; each page keeps its share for the next start.

The window Device shows the device on every page, above the window Configuration at first. The title bar of either moves it to another side of the window, next to the other one, or out of it as a window of its own (e.g. on another screen); View → Device closes and opens the device (Configuration always stays open). The GUI keeps where they are for the next start. Clicking a strip of it (or Left, Right, Home, End) shows its slot on the page Slots.

The drawing of the device shows the encoder with its ring of 13 LEDs (Mackie Control lights the middle 11), the LCD (the backlight in the strip's color shines around a dark panel and through its characters, as on the device), the meter next to Rec, Solo, Mute and Select, and the fader with its dB scale: the middle of the cap marks the value, -∞ at the bottom, 0 dB at 77 % of the travel (behavior.unity_at). What each slot shows is printed under its LCD.

The footer shows the problems, whether the device runs the file, the control Preview while there are unsaved changes or Simulate is open, and the buttons Undo, Redo, Revert and "Save and apply". The title of the window names the file, with • while there are unsaved changes. The header has the state of the service with buttons to install, start, restart or stop it (see The service), and what the sound server has.

Help where you look: while the mouse is on something with a tooltip, the footer shows its first sentence at once, in place of the status line; the tooltip itself follows after a moment, with the states, channels and slots it names in their colors. A pill with ▾ opens what it means in full on a click, with what can be done about it: a row per thing, with a bar in the color of how it does (a problem is also tinted and its fix is the main button). A control that is off says why next to it (e.g. "Play: device not connected").

States, channels and slots have a color each, in the whole window: states (and modes) violet, channels (and what else a slot can show: pools, people) teal, slots orange. The icons of their pages on the rail, the chips of the slots, the state bar and the words and sections in the help ([state.gaming], "the slot", "an application", apps) have them; a condition of presence (present) is yellow. The controls of the device (Select, Mute, the fader, the encoder, ...) stand out from the help in the color of the text.

Lists and pages that scroll cast a soft shadow at an edge where more of them is hidden, and popovers a shadow on the window under them.

The menus have what is used now and then: File (Save and apply, Revert, Quit), Edit (Undo, Redo), View (the window Device, the dark or the light theme, the zoom) and Help (this documentation).

items.title: The service
items.text:
The pill of the service in the header tells its state ("running", "stopped", "not installed", and the worst problem of a connection of the daemon). A click on it opens what goes with it: the service with Install and start, Start or Restart (the same as xtouch-daemon install-service) and, while it runs, Stop (systemctl --user stop: it stays enabled, so it starts again with the next session, or with "Start"); the unit systemd uses; and the connections of the daemon, each with its settings. Installing and starting ask first. What the service needs (Install and start, Start, or Restart after an upgrade) also has its button next to the pill.

A daemon that runs outside systemd (e.g. from a terminal or an IDE) is found too: the header shows "running elsewhere", and saving reloads it. The GUI does not start, restart or stop that one: restart it where it runs.

The unit is "packaged" for the one of the Arch Linux package (/usr/lib/systemd/user/xtouch-daemon.service), or "own unit" for a unit in ~/.config/systemd/user, which install-service wrote, e.g. for a checkout; the popover has its path and the program it starts.

  • Install and start takes the unit of the package when the GUI is the one of the package: it enables and starts it, and writes no file. Any other GUI writes a unit for its own xtouch-daemon to ~/.config/systemd/user.
  • Use the packaged unit shows while a unit in ~/.config/systemd/user overrides the one of the package. It removes that file; an enabled service stays enabled, and a running one restarts with the program of the package.
  • Restart stands out (with a tooltip that names both versions) when the daemon runs another version than the one installed, e.g. after an upgrade of the package: the daemon keeps running the old version until it restarts. This needs a daemon that tells its version (0.1.0 and later), and only counts for the service of the installation the GUI runs from.

items.title: Zoom
items.text:
Ctrl++ (or Ctrl+=) makes the whole window larger, Ctrl+- smaller, Ctrl+0 goes back to 100 %; View → Zoom has the levels from 67 % to 300 %. The GUI keeps the zoom for the next start, like the theme.

Qt scales a window only when it opens, so a new zoom opens the window again at the new size: unsaved changes, undo, the selected slot and the page stay. The zoom is on top of a QT_SCALE_FACTOR of the environment.

items.title: Live view
items.text:
While the daemon runs, the drawing shows what the device shows right now ("Live", in a pill on the right of the bar of the window Device), read from the daemon's live view. Without a running daemon the strips are dark and the pill says "No daemon": the drawing is the device, and only the daemon drives it. Start it (xtouch-daemon install-service --now), or use "Try without a device", which starts a daemon with the virtual device. A daemon that runs while the device is not connected shows "Live · not connected": the strips show what the device will show once it is there.

With the virtual device (run --virtual-device), the pill says "Live · virtual device" once the daemon drives it, and "virtual device not running · Open it" while the daemon waits for it: a click opens it in the window (see below).

Next to it, a pill shows the mode the device shows ("Mode: gaming", "No mode" while no mode is on, "· by hand" when it was picked by hand). A mode is a state with mode = true: one at a time is on. A click lists the states, with what turned each on, and picks a mode by hand ("Pick gaming", "Pick no mode", "Back to the rules").

The pill of the service at the top tells what the daemon is connected to: "running" while all is well, else the worst problem, e.g. "running · Home Assistant not authorized" or "running · device not connected". A click lists each connection (the device, the sound server, Home Assistant with an [mqtt] section, the voice chat with [voip]), how it is doing and why (for Home Assistant the broker's own words and what to check), with a button to its settings.

items.title: Select and Play
items.text:
A bar above the drawing of the device switches what the mouse does on it:

  • Select: a click picks a strip, and with it its slot on the page Slots. Dragging a strip moves its slot to another place: the strip lifts out of the row, the others glide aside, and a dashed place shows where it goes; Escape puts it back. Ctrl+Left/Right and the context menu (Move left, Move right) do the same. A slot takes its candidates ([slots]) and its controls ([controls]) along, the slots in between make room; Ctrl+Z moves it back. Comments above the slots in the file stay where they are.
  • Play: the mouse is a hand on the device, and the drawing looks like the device: no strip is selected, and there are no outlines of the selection, the focus or the mouse (the selection comes back with Select):
  • a fader: press to touch it, drag to move it, release to let go; Alt-drag moves it without a touch, like the device moving it by itself (the daemon puts it back);
  • a button: held while the mouse button is down;
  • an encoder: the wheel turns it (a touchpad too), and so does a drag on the knob (up or right turns it clockwise); a click pushes it, and holding the knob still holds it down; holding on an LED of the ring turns it until the ring lights that LED.

Play works on the virtual device the window hosts, and on the device of a running daemon: then the daemon takes what the mouse does as if the device sent it, so the mixer acts and a motorized fader follows once it is let go. The fader under the mouse is drawn there at once. While the drawing shows the preview in the GUI, Play acts on the virtual twin in the daemon (see Preview). Play is off without a daemon (or with one of another user, or too old to take it) and while the device is not connected; the bar says why next to it ("Play: device not connected"). With a daemon that drives the virtual device ([device] virtual = true) while it doesn't run, Play opens it in the window and plays on it.

While no daemon runs, "Try without a device" starts one with the virtual device on this file (saved first if it is new) and opens the device in the window, in Play: to set everything up and try it before there is a device. That daemon ends with the window.

items.title: The virtual device
items.text:
While the window hosts the virtual device, Play is on (see Select and Play).

A bar above the drawing unplugs it and plugs it in again, switches it off and on (the faders go down by themselves, as on the device), and breaks the touch sensor of faders ("Broken touch"), to try touchless_faders. "Close" closes it, and so does closing the window: for the daemon it is unplugged. What the drawing shows still comes from the daemon, which is what reached the device.

items.title: Preview
items.text:
Next to Save and apply, a pill says what the device runs: "Saved, on the device", "Unsaved changes" (the device runs the saved file), "In the GUI, not saved", "On the device, not saved", or what is wrong (e.g. "Not running", "Not on the device yet"). A click tells it in full, with the path of the file ("Copy the path", "Open the folder") and the file the daemon reads when that is another one.

While there are unsaved changes, or Simulate is open, the control "Preview" sits next to it. It decides where the changes (and Simulate, which always includes them) show before they are saved, a moment after each change (undo and redo too). The file is not written.

  • In the GUI (the default): the window shows the preview on a virtual twin of the device in the daemon. The twin is a second, complete set of strips that drives no real sound, voice chat, Home Assistant or device. The drawing, the cards of the page Slots and Play show the twin, with a frame around the drawing. Without Simulate, the twin runs the changes in the situation of now: the mode and the states the device has, and the applications, people and devices there are. The device keeps running the saved file. The pill says "In the GUI, not saved".
  • On the device: the device runs the preview, before it is saved: pick it to try the changes for real. The drawing shows the device, and the pill "On the device, not saved" ("Sending to the device…" for a moment after a change).
  • Off: the drawing shows the device as it is, running the saved file, for when you can't see the device. The changes show nowhere until you save them or pick another place. Opening Simulate moves the preview to In the GUI, and ending it back to Off.

The place stays as it is set for the next changes until the window closes; a new window starts with In the GUI.

  • Save and apply makes it the configuration: the daemon loads the saved file, which is what the preview showed.
  • Back to the file: another place, closing the window (it asks about unsaved changes as usual, and says when the device runs them) or "Revert" brings back the saved file. So does a window that crashed: the daemon goes back to the file when the connection of the window ends, or when the window does not answer for 10 seconds. On the device, the file also comes back when it changes on disk, or the daemon is reloaded; then the preview goes back to In the GUI and the window says why.
  • What the daemon does not take shows in red under the status bar at the top, and the preview keeps the version before. On the device it can't change [mqtt] (that takes a save and a restart), nor [device] name and virtual (they take a save). A configuration with problems is not sent at all: the pill says "Paused: problems" until they are fixed.
  • Channels, states and slots are all part of it: a stack changed in the editor shows in the preview as it is.
  • Simulate: its situation shows where the preview shows. On the device, the device shows the what-if of Simulate instead of what really happens: the states and the mode it sets, its channels present or absent, and its people, applications and devices (real ones first, so their faders move real audio; made-up ones for the rest, App 1, Device 1). Delays and dwells apply as they really do. The pill says "On the device · simulated". Home Assistant never sees it: its slot and state sensors stay as they really are, and nothing of it is kept.
  • One window on the device at a time: a second window that picks On the device takes over, and the first one's preview goes back to In the GUI.
  • Home Assistant: channels the changes do not have keep their entities in Home Assistant (with their state; only nothing drives them), so they are as before once the file runs again. Entities of channels only the changes had are removed again when it ends.

The places say why they are off in their tooltips: In the GUI needs a running daemon of your user; On the device also needs one that reads this file. A daemon from before this feature has neither (restart it to run the installed version).

items.title: The slots
items.text:
On the page Slots:

  • The state bar lists the states and modes: ● on, ○ off, with the override in brackets. A click on one shows what turned it on, its override (real, like Home Assistant or xtouch-daemon mode: auto, on, off, or for a mode picking it and back to the rules), and Simulate with it the other way (nothing changes).
  • A card per slot lists its candidates as rules, read from the top like "if, else if, else": the first whose condition holds wins. when gaming → auto shows auto while gaming is on, otherwise → browser below it browser the rest of the time (always for a lone candidate without a condition). A pool without a condition reads when app without a slot → apps (an outlined chip): it shows only while it has a member no other slot has, else the slot goes on to the next candidate. A tiny LCD after what it shows has the color of the strip: the candidate's own color, else the channel's or the pool's, else white (two for auto: applications and people; one per color for a pool of channels; dark for -). Its tooltip says where the color comes from. A rail on the left joins the candidates from the top, with "else" between two and a node on each: green on the one the device shows (or Simulate would). Above it, the candidates are dimmed with why they did not win (✗ browser doesn't play, ✗ browser is on slot 3); below it, dimmed more: not reached. When none of them has anything to show (e.g. the last is a pool with no member left), all are dimmed with why (✗ no person without a slot) and the rail ends in a row of its own, "nothing to show: the strip is dark", which is the one shown. On the one shown, the chip of a pool names what it hands out there (apps · firefox, people · Alice), and its tooltip who else waits for a slot. A card that gets a line more or less grows or shrinks smoothly. Conditions are outlined chips, what the slot shows a filled one. The states are violet (call, not gaming, one per or). present is spelled out in an olive chip (green in the light theme), in what it means for the type of the channel or pool: browser if present reads when browser plays → browser, mic if present mic is connected, mum if present mum is in the voice chat, present(people) someone is in the voice chat. What the slot shows is teal (see the colors), and the green node is on the row that shows (on people while a person sits there, also when apps is above it). Options of the strip in that slot only follow as in the file (color = white, rec = recording). + adds auto at the end, the bin (or Del) removes the candidate picked. Drag a candidate, or move it with Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down. A slot without candidates shows auto.
  • The inspector starts with the path of the slot's candidates (Slot 3 › 1 games › 2 apps: the one picked highlighted, ● the one the slot shows, ○ the one it came to that has none left; a click picks one) and a box of what goes on: why the slot shows what it shows, a step a line (✗ a candidate passed over and why, → what it shows, the same as xtouch-daemon why 3), which channel the candidate shows, where else that is used and where it is now, or what a pool hands out and from which side, with "Edit the channel" to its page, and what [controls] claims of the slot. Below it, it edits the candidate picked: what it shows (a channel, a pool such as apps, people or auto, -), when (the condition: states violet, channels in present(...) teal, a mistake underlined in red with what is wrong in its tooltip; typing offers the states, keywords and channels that fit, Ctrl+Space all of them), and the options of its place (look, on apps and auto the encoder and the volume range, on people the look of a person's strip).

Clicking a strip in the window Device (or Left, Right, Home, End) picks its card, with the candidate it shows.

Simulate shows what the slots would show in another mode, with other states on, with channels absent (auto plays: an application plays; people fill, apps fill: as many as there are slots), or with so many people in the call and applications that play (the two counts; the strips show their names). Simulate includes the unsaved changes and shows where the preview shows: in the GUI, on the virtual twin of the device in the daemon, or on the device. A frame goes around the drawing in the window Device, a bar of what-ifs replaces the state bar, and the drawing, the cards and the box of the inspector show it, and Play can operate it. Simulate needs a running daemon of your user: without one its button is off and says how to start it. Esc, or Simulate again, ends it.

items.title: Editing options
items.text:
The forms come from the options of the configuration, so every option has a field. The options of a channel are in cards in the order of the device, from top to bottom: what it controls, the encoder, the display, the buttons (Rec, Solo and Select each with what a press does, what a hold does and what the LED shows; unset, each shows the default of the type), the fader and the meter, then those about slots (tags, in_pool, ...).

The cards of the encoder, the display, the buttons and the fader have a drawing of that part of the strip, which shows what the options do on the device in a few steps (‹ and › go through them), each with a caption: the ring as the encoder turns and is pushed, the LCD while audio plays (with the label of each choice), while muted and with nothing to control, which LEDs light while audio plays, an application records or the strip is muted and after a press or a hold of each button that does something, and the volume at the bottom, at the 0 dB mark and at the top of the fader, with what the meter shows there. It follows the values in the form at once, saved or not, at the step shown.

  • switches for on/off options, numbers with their ranges, choices, color swatches, lists as chips, masked fields for secrets, and file pickers;
  • the help of each option under its field, with its default and, where the documentation explains more, a "Learn more" link to that section; a button sets the option back to its default;
  • choices (and profiles) as a list of entries, each with its label, its device and what it needs. The pencil or a double click opens an entry with its fields, with the devices, the sound cards and the profiles of its card to pick from; the card and the profile are under "Switch the sound card first". Drag ⠿ (or Ctrl+Up/Down) to change the order, which is the order Select goes through them. While a channel has choices, device and profiles are hidden, and the other way around: a channel has one or the other;
  • the meter as one choice: the level before the fader, after it, or off;
  • for choices, what the chosen value does (e.g. recording for the Rec LED), and each value says it as a tooltip in the list;
  • the mouse wheel scrolls the page, also over a number or a choice: it never changes a value;
  • the errors next to the options they belong to, with the same messages as xtouch-daemon check-config. The problems button in the footer lists them all; a click opens the page of the problem. An unknown option can be removed from there.

[mqtt] can be added and removed on its page. Above its options, the page shows how the daemon's connection is doing (or that the daemon runs without the section, which it reads only when it starts), and "Test connection" connects once with the settings as they are in the editor, saved or not, and says what is wrong if that fails.

items.title: Suggestions from the sound server
items.text:
The GUI reads the sound server and suggests what it has. A click into a field opens the list, and typing narrows it down (by any part of a name or a description, or a pattern with * and ?), with the parts that match highlighted; each line says what it is, where it is known from (the default, the active profile, a preset) and below it the name that goes into the option. Under device, card and profile of a choice, a line says what the value matches, e.g. "Matches 2: ..." for bluez_output.*, or "Matches nothing known" (a device can come later).

Option Suggestions device The outputs or inputs by node name, with their descriptions; the default is marked. Then the devices that another profile of their sound card would make (e.g. the digital output while the card is in its analog profile): picked for a choice, they fill in its card and profile. Then the devices the daemon saw that are not there now, e.g. Bluetooth headphones that are off ("seen 3 days ago"); Delete in the list forgets one. card, profile of a choice The sound cards (by description, or the devices they have), and the profiles of the card of the choice. profiles The profiles of the sound cards of those devices; the active one is marked. match, exclude of [pool.apps], apps and recording of a state The presets (@browsers, ...) first, then the names and binaries of the applications that play. A preset's tooltip tells what it stands for; its chip is outlined. processes of a state The presets for processes. [aliases] The names of the applications that play. person of a person channel The people in the voice chat now, as the running daemon tells them.

The pill "Sound server: ..." says how much the GUI read; a click lists the outputs, inputs and applications, with "Read again" (also the refresh button next to it), e.g. after you started an application. Without a sound server, type the names by hand. The people of the voice chat come from the daemon's live view: without a running daemon (or nobody in the channel), type the names by hand.

items.title: Undo
items.text:
Every edit can be undone: Ctrl+Z undoes, Ctrl+Shift+Z redoes. That includes removing a channel and reverting the file, so neither asks first. Typing into one option is one step. Ctrl+Z undoes in the document also while a text field has the focus.

Closing the window with unsaved changes asks whether to save them.

items.title: Keyboard
items.text:
Help → Keyboard shortcuts lists the keys. The keys of the menus follow the desktop; these are the usual ones:

Keys What they do Ctrl+S Save and apply Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z Undo, redo Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+4 Slots, Channels, States, Settings Del (or Backspace) Remove the candidate, channel, pool or state picked, as its button Remove does Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V Copy, cut, paste it Ctrl+D Duplicate it F2 Rename it: the focus goes to its id (on a candidate: to Shows) Ctrl+Up, Ctrl+Down Move the candidate picked, or the entry of a table Left, Right, Home, End Pick a strip of the drawing; Ctrl+Left, Ctrl+Right move its slot Esc End Simulate, close a popover

Del, Ctrl+C and the others of the menu Edit are for the list that has the focus: the cards on Slots, the lists on Channels and States. In a field they edit its text. Copy puts the entry on the clipboard as in the file: a channel as [channel.mic] with its options, a candidate as the value of the list of its slot ("browser if call"). Paste takes that back, also from a text editor, and gives a channel, pool or state whose id is taken one after it (mic_2). A candidate goes after the one picked; channels, pools and states go at the end.

items.title: Save and apply
items.text:
"Save and apply" (Ctrl+S) writes the file and reloads the daemon:

  • It saves only a file without problems: the daemon would not take one with problems.
  • Unchanged values keep their place and their comments, and a stack keeps its form (a string, a list, tables) where it did not change. The file is written in place, so a symlinked configuration stays one.
  • It reloads the running daemon when that reads the saved file: the service, or one started from a terminal or an IDE.
  • Without changes it is there too while the daemon runs another version of the file, e.g. one edited outside the GUI: then it only reloads the daemon.
  • A changed [mqtt] section is not reloaded at all: the window offers "Restart the service" for the service; restart a daemon that runs elsewhere where it runs. A changed [device] name or virtual is: the daemon switches to that device.
  • It then tells whether the device runs the saved file: "The device runs the saved file", or "The device does not run the saved file yet". If that stays, the daemon did not take the file, and its log says why (journalctl --user -u xtouch-daemon).

"Revert" drops the changes and reads the file again (Undo brings them back).

items.title: Changes of the file on disk
items.text:
The window notices when something else changes the file while it is open: an editor, a script, init-config.

  • Without unsaved changes it reads the file again. The page and the strip that were picked stay. Undo goes back to the version before, as changes to save.
  • With unsaved changes a bar above the page asks. Reload reads the file and drops the changes (Undo brings them back). Keep mine goes on with them, and the next save overwrites the file.
  • A file that can't be read (e.g. a TOML error) leaves the window as it is, and the bar says why. Once the file is fixed, the window reads it.
  • "Save and apply" never overwrites a change it did not show: if the file changed since the window read it, it asks first (Overwrite, Reload or Cancel).

Next: Commands for the same things on the command line, Troubleshooting.

items.title: Home Assistant
items.text: A homeassistant channel is a strip that belongs to Home Assistant instead of PipeWire: every part of it is an entity there, and automations decide what it does. For example, the fader dims a light, the encoder sets the volume of a speaker in another room, a button toggles a scene. The daemon reaches Home Assistant over MQTT discovery, so it needs the [mqtt] section.

items.title: PipeWire or Home Assistant?
items.text: Each control has one owner. The audio channels (output, input, apps) and the pools (auto, apps, ...) control audio on this computer and need nothing else. A homeassistant channel controls nothing by itself; it only reports what happens on it and shows what Home Assistant sets. In between, an audio channel can hand its fader or its encoder to Home Assistant and keep the other one for the volume, see below, and [controls] hands a control of a slot to Home Assistant whatever the slot shows. Never both on one control: a fader that both set a PipeWire volume and were moved by Home Assistant would fight over the motor.

items.title: [mqtt]
items.text:
The MQTT broker of Home Assistant, e.g. the Mosquitto add-on. Anything that is an entity in Home Assistant needs it (homeassistant channels and controls, homeassistant = true on a state); without such, the section is optional, and with it the daemon still shows the device, its modes, states and slots in Home Assistant.

Option Default Meaning host required The broker, e.g. "homeassistant.local". port 1883 Its port. username none The user to log in as. password none The password, in the file. password_file none A file that holds the password instead, e.g. one only you can read. ~ is the home directory. Surrounding whitespace is ignored. password_env none An environment variable that holds the password instead, e.g. set with systemctl --user edit xtouch-daemon (Environment=). discovery_prefix "homeassistant" Home Assistant's MQTT discovery prefix. namespace "xtouch" Starts every entity ID (number.xtouch_lamp_fader) and is part of the topics. Lower case letters, digits, _. device_name "X-Touch Extender" The name of the device in Home Assistant.

Set at most one of password, password_file and password_env. A password file that can't be read, or a variable that is not set, stops the daemon at the start with a message.

[mqtt]
host = "homeassistant.local"
username = "xtouch"
password_file = "~/.config/xtouch-daemon/mqtt-password"

A changed [mqtt] section needs a restart of the daemon (systemctl --user restart xtouch-daemon). Until then, a reload keeps the whole current configuration.

The entities are available in Home Assistant while the daemon runs and the device is connected; otherwise they are greyed out. A last will covers a crash. The daemon connects to the broker again by itself when it was gone.

The GUI shows whether the daemon is connected, and why not (e.g. a wrong password), and its "Test connection" button tries settings before they are saved.

items.title: homeassistant channels
items.text:
Option Default Meaning type required "homeassistant". label none The top line of the LCD until Home Assistant sets one, and the start of the entity names (the id without it). color "white" The LCD color until Home Assistant sets one. 
[mqtt]
host = "homeassistant.local"
username = "xtouch"
password_env = "XTOUCH_MQTT_PASSWORD"

[channel.living_room]
type = "homeassistant"   # number.xtouch_living_room_fader, ...
label = "Living"
color = "yellow"

[slots]
8 = "living_room"

The entities belong to the channel, not to a slot: they stay in Home Assistant whichever slot shows the channel, and while none does.

items.title: Audio strips with Home Assistant controls
items.text:
An output, input or apps channel with encoder = "homeassistant" or fader = "homeassistant" keeps the volume on the other control and gets these entities of the list below:

Option Entities encoder = "homeassistant" number.<ns>_<id>_encoder, and event.<ns>_<id>_buttons with encoder_pressed, encoder_released. fader = "homeassistant" number.<ns>_<id>_fader, and event.<ns>_<id>_buttons with fader_touched, fader_released. select = { press = "homeassistant" } (also rec, solo) event.<ns>_<id>_buttons with select_pressed, select_released.

The LCD and the LEDs stay with PipeWire, and so do the buttons unless they say homeassistant (see Buttons). The channel's id names the entities, its label starts their names. See Encoders for the details.

[channel.desk]
type = "output"
device = "alsa_output.usb-*"
label = "Desk"
encoder = "homeassistant"    # the fader sets the volume, the encoder dims the desk lamp

items.title: Controls of a slot
items.text:
A control of a slot can belong to Home Assistant whatever the slot shows, with [controls]: the fader, the encoder (turn and push), and the Select, Rec and Solo buttons (an event per press, and a select for the LED). The entities are named by the slot (number.xtouch_slot_6_fader), or by id:

[controls]
6 = { fader = "homeassistant", id = "desk" }      # number.xtouch_desk_fader
4 = { encoder = "homeassistant" }                 # number.xtouch_slot_4_encoder

With the fader taken, the encoder sets the volume of what the slot shows; with only the encoder taken, the fader keeps it.

items.title: Entities
items.text:
<ns> is mqtt.namespace, <id> the id of the channel (desk for [channel.desk]), or for a control of a slot its id or slot_<n>:

Entity What it is number.<ns>_<id>_fader The fader, 0..100 in steps of 0.1. Setting it moves the motor fader; moving the fader by hand sets it (at most every 100 ms while it moves, and where it was let go). number.<ns>_<id>_encoder The encoder, 0..100. The ring shows it; turning the encoder changes it by behavior.encoder_step per step. number.<ns>_<id>_meter The LED meter, 0..100 %: 0 is dark, 100 lights it fully; the daemon holds the level (the device would let it fall). Its 14 levels are about 7 % each, 100 % lights the red LED at the top too, so e.g. a CPU load or a power ratio goes in as it is. text.<ns>_<id>_top, text.<ns>_<id>_bottom The two lines of the LCD, 7 characters each. select.<ns>_<id>_color The LCD color: off, red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan, white. select.<ns>_<id>_rec_led, _solo_led, _mute_led, _select_led The LEDs of the buttons: off, on or flash. event.<ns>_<id>_buttons What happens on the strip: rec_pressed, rec_released, solo_…, mute_…, select_…, encoder_pressed, encoder_released, fader_touched, fader_released.

A button does not switch its LED: if a button should toggle something, an automation reacts to the event and sets the LED to show the result. Home Assistant keeps what it set last (retained on the broker), so after a restart of the daemon the strips show it again. New entities start with the configured label and color, the fader and encoder at 0 and the LEDs off. While the broker can't be reached, a strip shows its label, offline and its color, and the device does nothing on it.

Entities of a channel that was removed from the configuration are removed from Home Assistant on the next reload.

items.title: Choices
items.text:
With [mqtt], an output or input channel with choices has select.<ns>_<id>_output (select.<ns>_<id>_input): the choice the strip shows, one option per choice, named by its label (or its device; a second choice of the same name gets a number, e.g. Out 2). Choosing one switches to it like Select on the device, profile first; one that isn't there is refused and the select goes back. The select follows the strip, also when the default changes elsewhere.

action: select.select_option
target:
  entity_id: select.xtouch_out_output
data:
  option: Speaker

items.title: Modes, states and slots
items.text:
With [mqtt], Home Assistant sees and sets the states and modes:

Entity What it is select.<ns>_mode The mode picked by hand, or auto for the rules. Choosing one picks it, like xtouch-daemon mode. binary_sensor.<ns>_state_<id> Each state and mode, with the attributes since, source and override. select.<ns>_state_<id> The override of each state that is no mode: auto, on, off. switch.<ns>_state_<id>_input For states with homeassistant = true: what Home Assistant feeds into them. binary_sensor.<ns>_<id>_shown Whether a channel is on a slot. sensor.<ns>_slot_<n> What slot n shows (a channel id, app:<name>, person:<name> or none), with label, kind, via and reason.

For example, the mode gaming while the PC runs a game, from another room's automation:

action: select.select_option
target:
  entity_id: select.xtouch_mode
data:
  option: gaming

items.title: Automations
items.text:
An automation that dims a light with the fader, shows its brightness on the LCD, and toggles it with Mute:

automation:
  - alias: "X-Touch: fader dims the living room"
    mode: queued
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: number.xtouch_living_room_fader
    actions:
      - action: light.turn_on
        target: { entity_id: light.living_room }
        data:
          brightness_pct: "{{ trigger.to_state.state | float | round(0) }}"
      - action: text.set_value
        target: { entity_id: text.xtouch_living_room_bottom }
        data:
          value: "{{ trigger.to_state.state | float | round(0) }}%"

  - alias: "X-Touch: Mute toggles the living room"
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: event.xtouch_living_room_buttons
        attribute: event_type
        to: mute_pressed
    actions:
      - action: light.toggle
        target: { entity_id: light.living_room }

  - alias: "X-Touch: the Mute LED shows the living room light"
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: light.living_room
    actions:
      - action: select.select_option
        target: { entity_id: select.xtouch_living_room_mute_led }
        data:
          option: "{{ 'on' if is_state('light.living_room', 'on') else 'off' }}"

  - alias: "X-Touch: the meter shows the power of the washing machine"
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: sensor.washing_machine_power
    actions:
      - action: number.set_value
        target: { entity_id: number.xtouch_living_room_meter }
        data:
          # 2000 W lights it fully
          value: "{{ [trigger.to_state.state | float(0) / 2000 * 100, 100] | min | round(0) }}"

To react to the entities from code, see As a haad controller.

Next: Slots (controls of a slot), Troubleshooting.

items.title: Mumble
items.text:
With the Mumble plugin of xtouch-daemon, the strips of people show the people in your Mumble channel, one per strip:

  • the name on the LCD, the backlight in talking_color while they talk, and their voice on the meter;
  • the fader sets their volume for you (0 to 200 %, max_volume at the top);
  • Mute mutes them for you: it is Mumble's own local mute, so Mumble shows it, and a local mute you set in Mumble lights the button;
  • people who join or leave the channel, and you moving to another channel, show at once.

It needs Mumble 1.4 or later on Linux (x86_64). People sit on the slots of auto (and people) in every configuration; the [voip] section can be left out: its provider = "bridge" is the default.

items.title: Setup in the GUI
items.text:
The page Settings, Voice chat (the [voip] section) has a box "Mumble":

  1. Click Install Mumble plugin. It copies the plugin into Mumble's plugin directory (~/.local/share/Mumble/Mumble/Plugins, or the one of the Flatpak), replacing an older one. (Without a plugin to install, e.g. in a checkout, the button builds it first; that needs cmake and a C compiler.) Mumble's own installer is not used: with a Mumble that runs, it starts a second instance, which crashed (Mumble 1.5.939).
  2. In Mumble: Settings, Plugins, click Reload plugins (or restart Mumble), tick Enable of "xtouch-daemon", and Apply.
  3. Keep provider = "bridge" (the default). People take free auto (and people) slots from the right; see the example below.
  4. Join a channel. The pill of the box says Mumble connected and how many people are in the channel.

The pill shows what the running daemon sees: "waiting for Mumble" while the plugin is not connected (Mumble is not running, or the plugin is not enabled), "not in use" for a daemon older than the people of auto.

items.title: Setup on the command line
items.text:
xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin --install

does what the button does (see mumble-plugin); then step 2 above. Without xtouch-daemon's help: in Mumble, Settings, Plugins, Install plugin..., and pick /usr/share/xtouch-daemon/xtouch-daemon.mumble_plugin (a release) or integrations/mumble/build/xtouch-daemon.mumble_plugin (a checkout, after xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin --build).

items.title: Slots for Mumble
items.text:
Alice always on slot 1 while she is there, the others on the auto slots from the right, and Mumble as one strip with your microphone while you are in a channel:

[channel.alice]
type = "person"
person = "Alice"      # her name in Mumble

[channel.voip]
type = "apps"
match = ["mumble"]
label = "Mumble"

[channel.mic]
type = "input"

[state.call]
voice_chat = true     # in a channel of Mumble
delay_off = 5

[slots]
1 = ["alice if present", "auto"]
6 = ["voip if call", "auto"]
7 = ["mic if call", "auto"]

See People and the voice chat and States and modes.

To start Mumble from the device, give a slot a launch in [controls] with a mumble:// URL, e.g. 6 = { select = { launch = ["mumble", "mumble://me@voice.example.org/Gaming"] }, when = "not call" }: Select starts Mumble, which connects to the server and joins the channel. See Launching the application.

items.title: Behavior and limits
items.text:
• Mute is Mumble's "Local Mute" (in the menu of a user): Mute on the strip sets it, Mumble shows it in its window, and setting it in Mumble lights the button. Mumble tells plugins of no change of the local mute, so the plugin looks every half second: a mute set in Mumble reaches the button within about 0.5 s (a press of Mute on the strip shows at once). Should Mumble refuse a mute, the button goes back, and Mumble's log says why ("xtouch-daemon: can't mute ..."). A local mute set from the strip lasts while the person stays; Mumble only stores the ones set in its own menu (for registered users).
  • The volume is the plugin's own. The plugin scales the voice of each person before Mumble mixes it. Mumble's own "Local Volume Adjustment" is separate, and the faders don't show or change it: Mumble's plugin interface has no call for it. The two multiply: a person at 50 % in Mumble and 50 % on the fader is at 25 %.
  • The daemon keeps them for the name. The plugin forgets the volume of someone who leaves; the daemon remembers the volume and the mute the strips set for each name while it runs and sends them again when the person comes back (a mute changed in Mumble meanwhile replaces the one of the strip). A restart of the daemon starts everyone at 100 %.
  • Not their own mute. Whether other people muted or deafened themselves is not in Mumble's plugin interface: it tells their talking state only, and someone who muted themselves sends nothing, so they just don't talk.
  • Your channel only, without you: nobody else's channel, no whispers to other channels.
  • The level on the meter is the voice as it arrives, before or after the fader (meter_point), and before Mumble's own volume and positional audio. Mumble does not fetch the voice of a muted person: before the fader their meter lights while they talk, without a level; after it, it stays dark.

items.title: Flatpak
items.text:
A Mumble in a Flatpak can't see the socket by default. Let it:

flatpak override --user --filesystem=xdg-run/xtouch-daemon-voip.sock info.mumble.Mumble

How the plugin works and how to build it: Mumble plugin.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
"waiting for Mumble" although Mumble runs: check that the plugin is enabled in Mumble's settings (Plugins), and that xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin says "In Mumble: ..." with a path. The daemon logs "Voice chat plugin connected (mumble)" when it connects.

Nobody on the strips: the strips show your channel without you; join a channel with other people. People need free auto slots, or person channels on slots (xtouch-daemon check-config shows which slots are auto).

Two Mumble clients at once (e.g. a second one with mumble -m -c <other settings file> to test with another user): enable the plugin in one of them only. The daemon keeps the plugin that connected first and refuses the other one; it logs "Refusing another voice chat plugin while one is connected" once.

Next: Applications (start Mumble with Select), People (where people sit).

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
Start with the log and the state of the service:

systemctl --user status xtouch-daemon      # is the device, the sound server, the broker connected?
journalctl --user -u xtouch-daemon -f      # the log

For more detail, stop the service and run the daemon in the foreground with xtouch-daemon run -l debug.

items.title: The device
items.text:
The device shows IP: 192.168.001.100 wait.... It is set to its network interface and ignores USB. Switch it to MC mode on USB in its setup menu, see Getting started.

... is it switched on, in MC mode on USB? xtouch-daemon test can't find the sound card of the extender. The daemon waits for it and connects when it appears. Check that it is connected and on, and that /proc/asound/cards lists it. If the name differs, set [device] name to a part of it.

can't open X-Touch-Ext (... Device or resource busy). Only one program can use the device. Stop the daemon before xtouch-daemon test (systemctl --user stop xtouch-daemon), and close DAWs or other MIDI tools that opened it.

... Permission denied. Your user can't open the MIDI device in /dev/snd. Desktop sessions give access to the logged-in user; without a session, add the user to the audio group. See Hardware.

A fader does not change the volume. Only a touched fader changes a value. A fader whose touch sensor failed goes back to its value after a move. xtouch-daemon test shows whether the device reports fader touched. Until the sensor is repaired, touchless_faders makes the fader work without it.

A fader jumps on its first move after the daemon started. The device can't tell where its faders are, so after a connect the daemon assumes them at the bottom. A fader moved while the daemon did not run jumps from where it really is. See Hardware.

items.title: Audio
items.text:
The meters stay dark. A meter shows a level only while something plays to the output or records from the input. That is on purpose: the meters never open a device themselves. A microphone meter moves only while an application records from it. Check also behavior.meters and the strip's meter.

Streams don't follow when I select another output. Select makes the device the default, and streams without a fixed target follow the default. A stream that another tool moved to a particular device (pavucontrol's per-stream output menu, pactl move-sink-input) stays there. Move it back in pavucontrol, or restart the application's stream.

A strip shows off. The device it controls is not there, e.g. Bluetooth headphones that are switched off. It comes back by itself. xtouch-daemon list-devices shows the devices that are there.

An apps channel shows idle. No stream of its applications is there. xtouch-daemon list-apps shows the names and binaries of the applications that play, and which channel or slot takes each one.

Select does not start the application of launch. The daemon's log says why: a program that is not in PATH (can't launch ...), or one that did not show up in 15 s. Nothing happens either while the strip counts it as running: on apps channels also a process whose name contains a match entry (ps -eo comm shows them). The application's own output is in journalctl --user -u 'xtouch-launch-*'. A graphical application that finds no display there needs the desktop's variables in the systemd user manager (systemctl --user show-environment should list WAYLAND_DISPLAY or DISPLAY); most desktops import them at login.

An application lands on the wrong strip. xtouch-daemon list-apps names the channel or slot that takes it. An apps channel takes every application whose name or binary contains one of its match entries, so a short entry can match more than intended. check-config shows what the presets in match stand for.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
A slot shows something else than I expected. xtouch-daemon why 3 says why slot 3 shows what it shows, and why not each candidate above it; xtouch-daemon why browser where the channel is and why not elsewhere. The GUI shows the same in the inspector of the slot. xtouch-daemon check-config shows what the slots show in each situation.

A change does not show on the device. The daemon takes a saved file a moment later. A file with errors is logged and the old configuration stays: run xtouch-daemon check-config. A changed [mqtt] section needs a restart. The GUI tells whether the device runs the saved file.

items.title: Home Assistant
items.text:
The entities are unavailable. They are available only while the daemon runs and the device is connected. Check the broker settings in [mqtt] and the log. The GUI tells how the connection is doing in the popover of the service pill, and on the page Settings, Home Assistant, where "Test connection" tries the settings.

A strip shows offline. The broker can't be reached. The daemon connects again by itself.

items.title: Voice chat
items.text: "waiting for Mumble", or nobody on the strips. See Mumble: the plugin must be enabled in Mumble, and people need free auto slots or person channels on slots.

items.title: GUI
items.text:
xtouch-daemon gui says how to install it. The GUI is an extra (xtouch-daemon[gui], or xtouch-daemon-gui-bin on Arch), see Install.

The service pill says "unavailable". The daemon is not running as a systemd user service. Start it with systemctl --user start xtouch-daemon, or run it in the foreground. The GUI edits the file without it, and "Try without a device" needs none.

"The device does not run the saved file yet" stays. The daemon did not take the file; its log says why (journalctl --user -u xtouch-daemon).

Next: Commands, Hardware and protocol.

items.title: Commands
items.text:
Command What it does xtouch-daemon run Runs the daemon in the foreground. xtouch-daemon check-config Validates the configuration, describes its channels and shows what the slots show when. xtouch-daemon init-config Writes the example configuration. xtouch-daemon list-devices Lists outputs, inputs, and the sound cards with their profiles. xtouch-daemon list-apps Lists the applications that play, and which channel or slot takes each one. xtouch-daemon test Tests the LCDs, LEDs, rings, meters and faders, then shows what happens on the device. xtouch-daemon virtual-device Runs a virtual X-Touch Extender, for trying the daemon without the device. xtouch-daemon mode Shows the running daemon's mode, or picks another one. xtouch-daemon why Says why a slot shows what it shows, or where a channel is and why. xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin Shows, builds or installs the Mumble plugin for the strips of people. xtouch-daemon install-service Sets the daemon up as a systemd user service. xtouch-daemon gui Edits the configuration in a window. xtouch-daemon simulate What the slots of a configuration show in a situation you give it. xtouch-daemon observe Records what plays, records and runs, for simulate --replay.

Every command takes -h/--help. xtouch-daemon -V (--version) shows the version.

-c FILE (--config FILE) selects the configuration file; the default is ~/.config/xtouch-daemon/config.toml.

items.title: run
items.text:
xtouch-daemon run [-c FILE] [-l LEVEL] [--virtual-device]

Runs the daemon in the foreground. install-service sets it up as a systemd user service instead.

Option Meaning -c, --config FILE The configuration file. -l, --log-level LEVEL debug, info (default), warning or error. debug also logs the messages of the device the daemon doesn't use. --virtual-device Drives the virtual device instead of the real one, as [device] virtual = true.

The daemon notes its process and configuration file in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon.json while it runs, and serves what the device shows on $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon.sock for the GUI. A second daemon does not start: it names the one that runs.

Signals:

Signal Effect SIGHUP Reloads the configuration (systemctl --user reload xtouch-daemon), as the daemon does by itself when the file changes. A file with errors is logged, and the current configuration stays. SIGTERM, SIGINT Stops: the strips go dark from the right and the faders go down.

items.title: check-config
items.text:
xtouch-daemon check-config [-c FILE] [--all]

Validates the configuration, describes each channel and shows a table of what the slots show in which states. Without a file at the default path it checks the defaults. Example output:

/home/me/.config/xtouch-daemon/config.toml: valid
Channels:
  out: 'Speaker' output alsa_output.pci-0000_11_00.4.analog-stereo, select makes it the default (cyan, rec: recording, solo: off, encoder: balance)
  mic: the default input (red, rec: recording, solo: off, encoder: balance)
  browser: 'Browser' applications @browsers (firefox, chromium, ...) (yellow, rec: recording, solo: off, encoder: media)
  lamp: 'Living' Home Assistant, entities *.*_lamp_* (yellow)
What the slots show:
when     1    2        3     4-8
default  out  browser  auto  auto
call     out  browser  mic   auto

A channel with choices lists them, e.g. output: Phones, Speaker or Buds (Select switches). A channel whose meter shows the level after its fader (meter_point = "post_fader", see Meters) says meter post-fader.

A table of more than 12 rows shows the situations that differ in one thing; --all shows every combination.

A file with errors names the place of each one and its line in the file, e.g. channel.mic (line 12): label: String should have at most 7 characters, with what is likely meant where it can be guessed (browsr is no channel or pool (did you mean browser?)), and the command fails. After the table, Notes: lists candidates that can never show (e.g. a channel below a pool without a condition) and people with no slot to sit on.

items.title: init-config
items.text:
xtouch-daemon init-config [PATH] [-f]

Writes the example configuration with channels, states and slots to ~/.config/xtouch-daemon/config.toml, or to PATH. An existing file stays, unless -f (--force) overwrites it.

items.title: list-devices
items.text:
xtouch-daemon list-devices [--snippet]

Lists the outputs and inputs with the node names to use as device, their descriptions, volumes and states; * marks the defaults. Then it lists each sound card by its name and description, with its devices and its profiles (name and description), for card and profile of choices and for profiles; * marks the active ones. --snippet prints a [channel.<id>] for each device instead, ready to paste into the file (Bluetooth devices by a wildcard like bluez_output.*, since their names hold the address of the device):

Profiles of alsa_card.pci-0000_11_00.4, Family 17h/19h HD Audio Controller (alsa_output.pci-0000_11_00.4.analog-stereo):
  * output:analog-stereo+input:analog-stereo
      Analog Stereo Output + Analog Stereo Input
    output:iec958-stereo+input:analog-stereo
      Digital Stereo (IEC958) Output + Analog Stereo Input

items.title: list-apps
items.text:
xtouch-daemon list-apps [-c FILE]

Lists the applications that play now: their names (and aliases), the presets they are part of (e.g. Brave (@browsers)), binaries and volumes, and where each one goes: the apps channel that has it, an auto or apps slot, "ignored" (exclude of [pool.apps]) or no slot. Use the names and binaries, or the presets, for match, exclude and [aliases].

items.title: test
items.text:
xtouch-daemon test [-c FILE] [--no-events] [--virtual-device]

Lights up everything on the device and moves the faders: every strip lights its LCD in a color, its LEDs, ring and meter, and moves its fader up and down. Then it shows what you do on the device (faders, touches, buttons, encoders), and the messages from the device the daemon doesn't use, until Ctrl+C. --no-events ends after the test.

It takes the name of the device from [device] of the configuration. Stop the daemon first (systemctl --user stop xtouch-daemon): only one program can use the device. --virtual-device (or [device] virtual = true) tests the virtual device, which has to run (in another terminal).

items.title: virtual-device
items.text:
xtouch-daemon virtual-device [--broken-touch 1,4] [--log-level debug]

A virtual X-Touch Extender, for trying the daemon without the device: xtouch-daemon run --virtual-device (or [device] virtual = true) drives it instead of the real one, and the GUI shows what it shows. It runs headless until interrupted (Ctrl+C); the GUI can host one itself, with the mouse on its strips. One daemon at a time can use it.

Option Meaning --broken-touch The faders (from 1) whose touch sensor failed: they never report a touch, see Motor faders. --log-level debug also logs every message of the daemon.

items.title: mode
items.text:
xtouch-daemon mode [NAME | auto | --next | --previous]

Without arguments it prints the modes of the running daemon, marks the one that is on, and says whether it was picked by hand. mode gaming picks the mode gaming, --next and --previous the one after or before it, auto lets the rules decide again. It talks to the daemon over its live view socket, so it needs a running daemon.

items.title: why
items.text:
xtouch-daemon why SLOT | CHANNEL

Asks the running daemon why a slot (its number, 1 for the leftmost one) shows what it shows: why not each candidate above, and what it shows. For a channel (its id) it tells on which slots it is and why not on the others that ask for it:

$ xtouch-daemon why 2
Slot 2: voip if call: doesn't hold (call is off); shows auto:app:firefox
$ xtouch-daemon why browser
browser: on slot 4; not slot 8 (on slot 4 (tie, to the left))

The GUI shows the same above the inspector of a slot on the page Slots.

items.title: mumble-plugin
items.text:
xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin [--build] [--install]

The Mumble plugin that gives the strips of people the people of your Mumble channel. Without options it tells where the plugin is, whether Mumble is installed, and whether Mumble has the plugin:

Plugin: /usr/share/xtouch-daemon/xtouch-daemon.mumble_plugin
Mumble: installed
In Mumble: /home/me/.local/share/Mumble/Mumble/Plugins/libxtouch-daemon.so
Option Meaning --install Copies the plugin into Mumble's plugin directory (native, else the Flatpak's), replacing an older one; then Mumble needs "Reload plugins". Without a plugin it builds one first. --build Builds the plugin from the sources of a checkout (integrations/mumble, needs cmake and a C compiler) into integrations/mumble/build/. With --install: builds it again first.

A release has the plugin in /usr/share/xtouch-daemon/; a checkout builds it.

items.title: install-service
items.text:
xtouch-daemon install-service [--now] [--remove-override]

Writes the systemd user unit ~/.config/systemd/user/xtouch-daemon.service for the installed xtouch-daemon and reloads systemd. --now also enables and starts it. The unit is Type=notify, reloads with SIGHUP and restarts on failure.

The Arch Linux package installs its unit as /usr/lib/systemd/user/xtouch-daemon.service. Its xtouch-daemon install-service writes no file then: it reloads systemd, and with --now enables and starts that unit. A unit in ~/.config/systemd/user overrides the one of the package (systemd prefers it), e.g. one written before by a checkout; the command says so.

Option Meaning --now Also enable and start the service. --remove-override Only remove ~/.config/systemd/user/xtouch-daemon.service, so the unit of the package is in effect. An enabled service stays enabled, and a running one restarts with the program of the package.

Logs: journalctl --user -u xtouch-daemon -f.

items.title: gui
items.text:
xtouch-daemon gui [-c FILE]

Edits the configuration in a window, and applies it. Needs the gui extra, or the package xtouch-daemon-gui-bin (which has the command xtouch-daemon-gui). See GUI.

items.title: simulate
items.text:
xtouch-daemon simulate FILE [--mode NAME] [--state NAME]... [--absent CHANNEL]... [--playing APP]... [--person NAME]... [--table | --replay LOG]

What the 8 slots of FILE show in the given states, and why not the candidates above (see Channels, states and slots).

Option Meaning --mode, --state The mode and the states that are on; the others are off. --absent A channel that is not present; the others are. --playing, --person The applications that play (in the order they started) and the people in the voice chat, for the pools auto and people. --table Every combination of the states and presence the stacks ask about that changes what the slots show. --replay LOG Instead: replays observations recorded by observe through FILE. Prints when states and slots changed, how often each slot changed, the flaps (a slot back to what it showed within 60 s) and how long each state was on.

items.title: observe
items.text:
xtouch-daemon observe LOG [--interval 2.0] [--process NAME]...

Records, every --interval seconds, what plays and records on the sound server, the devices, the running processes (those of the presets, and --process) and the voice chat of the running daemon, and appends a line of JSON to LOG when that changed. Runs until interrupted (Ctrl+C). simulate FILE --replay LOG replays it.

items.title: Hardware and protocol
items.text:
The Behringer X-Touch Extender has 8 strips. Each has a 100 mm motorized, touch-sensitive fader, four buttons with LEDs (Rec, Solo, Mute, Select), an encoder with a push button and an LED ring, an LED meter, and an LCD with two lines of 7 characters and one of 8 backlight colors.

The meter has 8 LEDs: seven for the level (green, then orange) and a red clip LED at the top. Mackie Control sets it in 14 levels, about two per LED (only the 14th lights the clip LED), and the device lets it fall by itself. What the levels mean on an audio strip, and whether they are taken before or after the fader, is in Meters.

xtouch-daemon drives it over USB in its Mackie Control mode, so it acts as the "host" a DAW would be. The device needs no driver: it is a USB class compliant MIDI device.

First steps sets the device up (MC mode on USB) and tests it.

items.title: Linux access
items.text:
Linux lists the extender as a sound card (/proc/asound/cards: XTouchExt ... X-Touch-Ext) with the raw MIDI device /dev/snd/midiC<card>D0. xtouch-daemon finds the card by its name ([device] name) and opens that device directly, without ALSA sequencer or JACK.

The user needs read and write access to it. Desktop sessions give it to the logged-in user through the seat (logind). Without a session, add the user to the audio group.

Only one program can have the device open. Stop the daemon before xtouch-daemon test, and close DAWs that use it.

items.title: Motor faders
items.text:
• Touch: while a finger is on a fader, its motor does not follow outside changes. When the fader is let go, it moves to the strip's current value, usually the one that was set last.
  • Only a touched fader sets a value: the device reports a touch about 50-100 ms after the first moves of a quick hand. A move without a touch waits for one for 0.3 s with the motor still: with a touch it was the hand and counts, without one it was the device itself (e.g. its faders going down after it was switched on), and the fader goes back to its value. A fader whose touch sensor failed can't change the volume until it is repaired, or until it is one of the touchless_faders. With touch_required = false, every move of every fader counts.
  • Smooth motion: a fader glides to a new value instead of jumping there. It follows its target like a critically damped spring (no overshoot) that gets there in about 100 ms, starting from where it is, also from where a hand left it. The spring keeps its speed when the target moves on, so a volume dragged in another mixer, which arrives in small steps, becomes one even movement.
  • Arriving: once a fader is there, its value is sent twice more (after 0.15 s and 0.4 s), in case the motor stopped short of it. Stopping the daemon waits for that.
  • Slow moves: the big moves glide three times slower, and stay slow until the fader arrived: a fader that is put away because its strip goes dark (the daemon stops, an application ended, a reload), and the first move after a connect. After a fast move the motor stops a little short of the bottom; a slow one gets there. Tried on the device: neither sending the value again nor a nudge (a little up, then down again) did as well.
  • Startup and shutdown sequences: after a connect the strips light up and their faders come up; when the daemon stops they go dark and their faders go down. By default one after the other, from the left and from the right; [device] startup and shutdown choose others, see Startup and shutdown sequences. The device can't blink a ring and has no brightness levels, so the light effects are steps of on and off.
  • Start: the device can't tell where its faders are. It reports a position only while a finger moves a fader, not after a connect, not on the device query, not after a motor move. So after a connect a fader is assumed at the bottom, where the daemon leaves the faders when it stops, and glides from there. If it was moved while the daemon did not run, its first step jumps from where it really is.
  • Motor noise: slight steps can be heard while a fader moves, more above about 70 %. They come from the device, not from the values sent: a perfectly even 14-bit ramp at 100 Hz sounds the same. The motor control works in small steps (the positions the device reports are multiples of 4, so 12 bits), and the slider has play on its rail: the belt tilts it one way going up and the other way going down, which clicks. Don't grease it: the touch sensing goes through the knob and slider.
  • Fast moves: the device sends many positions per second. Only the latest one is set when the previous command finished, so a slow sound server does not build a queue.

items.title: The virtual device
items.text:
xtouch-daemon virtual-device and the GUI simulate the device (simulator/device.py), byte for byte, on a Unix socket in the runtime directory instead of /dev/snd. The daemon keeps the same model as a mirror of the real device, which is what the GUI draws. What it does like the device, as described on this page: the messages of Protocol both ways, the LCD as two lines of characters across the strips, a touch on a fader, positions reported in steps of 4, the motor that moves only when the host sets a value or a finger lets go, never under a finger, a fader whose touch sensor failed (no touch reported), and switching it off and on (its query, everything dark, the faders going down by themselves and reporting it).

What is assumed: how fast the motor goes (0.1 s over the whole travel), how fast a meter falls (one level per 0.15 s), and when the touch of a quick hand comes (70 ms after its first move).

items.title: Protocol
items.text: The Mackie Control protocol; the extender is an MCU XT (model id 0x15). Verified on the device (2026-11-15) unless marked otherwise. n is the strip, 0..7.

items.title: From the device
items.text: Element Message Host query F0 00 00 66 15 01 <7 byte serial> <4 byte challenge> F7, sent on its own after start. The device works without an answer. Fader Pitch bend on channel n: En lsb msb, 14 bits (0x0000..0x3FFF) Fader touch Note 0x68 + n, velocity 7F touched, 00 released Buttons Note on, velocity 7F pressed, 00 released: Rec 0x00 + n, Solo 0x08 + n, Mute 0x10 + n, Select 0x18 + n Encoder turn CC 0x10 + n: 01..3F clockwise, 41..7F counter-clockwise (the low 6 bits are the steps) Encoder push Note 0x20 + n

items.title: To the device
items.text:
Element Message Fader motor Pitch bend, like the fader position Button LEDs Note of the button, velocity 7F on, 01 flashing, 00 off LED ring CC 0x30 + n, value 0x40 (center LED) | mode << 4 (0 dot, 1 boost/cut, 2 wrap, 3 spread) | position 0 (off) or 1..11. The ring has 13 LEDs: the positions light the middle 11, and Mackie Control's center LED (0x40) lights the two at the ends, together. Meter Channel pressure D0, value n << 4 \| level, level 0..14. One more of the 8 LEDs every two levels (1–2 light one, 9–10 five), 11 lights six, 12–13 seven, 14 all eight with the red one at the top. 15 lights none. The device lets every level fall by itself (14 too: there is no overload LED it holds, unlike Mackie Control's 0x0E), so it must be sent again to hold a level. LCD text F0 00 00 66 15 12 <offset> <ASCII> F7, offset line * 56 + n * 7 LCD colors F0 00 00 66 15 72 <8 colors> F7 (a Behringer extension, works in MC mode): 0 black, 1 red, 2 green, 3 yellow, 4 blue, 5 magenta, 6 cyan, 7 white

The codec is in hardware/protocol.py: pure functions that decode the device's messages into events and build the messages that drive it.

Messages the daemon does not use are not lost: xtouch-daemon test prints them (unknown message: ...), and the daemon logs them at debug level (xtouch-daemon run -l debug). They show what a device sends that differs from the table above, e.g. a touch that is not the usual note.

See Troubleshooting for problems with the device.

items.title: The voice chat bridge
items.text:
What a plugin of a voice chat client (see People) and the daemon say to each other, for a plugin of another client than Mumble.

The daemon serves the Unix socket $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon-voip.sock (mode 0600). When a plugin connects, the daemon says who it is and which version of the protocol it speaks:

{"daemon": "xtouch-daemon", "version": "0.1.0", "protocol": 1}

The plugin sends its whole state on every change (and while someone talks, for the levels, e.g. 20 times a second), one JSON object per line:

{"protocol": 1, "client": "mumble", "channel": "Lobby", "capabilities": ["volume", "mute", "levels"],
 "participants": [{"id": "12", "name": "Alice", "talking": true, "muted": false, "volume": 100, "level": 0.4}]}

id and name are needed, the rest is optional; without protocol it is 1. channel is the channel the user is in (the GUI shows it). volume is 0..200 percent, level 0..1. capabilities says what the plugin can do: volume (the faders set volumes), mute (Mute mutes), levels (it sends level). The daemon sends commands back the same way:

{"set_volume": {"id": "12", "volume": 80}}
{"set_muted": {"id": "12", "muted": true}}

One plugin at a time: a new connection replaces the one before. When the plugin goes, so do the participants.

Versions. Both sides ignore keys they don't know, so new optional keys keep the version. A change that an older side would get wrong gets a new protocol number; the daemon ignores (and logs) the lines of a protocol it does not speak, so a plugin can tell from the greeting whether to speak an older one.
